An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds with 0.047 picoseconds in uncertainty. LHCb was able to achieve better precision in this measurement compared to its previous counterparts due to the larger number of $B^0_s\KK$ decay events observed, and it also enabled a more accurate assessment of direct $CP$ violation within the $\pp$ system.

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was first reported in 2011; however, a second anisotropy pattern emerged for energies beyond 8 EeV that required further investigation. By integrating prior measurement techniques with contemporary data from 2014-2015, we determined the anisotropy patterns reported at both the low and high energy extremes of our range. The spatial distribution of the low-energy anisotropy aligns with previously reported findings, whereas the location of the high-energy anisotropy matches earlier observations at the 2.6$\sigma$ level. The position of the cosmic ray distribution's centroid becomes increasingly dependent on the primary particle type and its momentum distribution as the energy level rises. We also re-examined the anisotropy patterns in terms of the orientation of the cosmic ray sources relative to the Milky Way, the Local Group, and the Virgo cluster, with the latter two showing the most favorable anisotropy results.

Owing to its sophisticated design and reliability, the ATLAS detector successfully collected a comprehensive dataset during heavy ion and proton-proton runs, yielding results in line with previous measurements from the CMS, ALICE, and LHCb collaborations. Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra or its universal enveloping algebra. By establishing a family of deformations within the algebra of polynomial functions, this study focuses on a simple Lie algebra and its envelope algebra, allowing for a set of differential and integral operations to be formed. These operations allow for the construction of deformed Fourier transforms and Weyl symbols, which in turn enable the study of Weyl calculus in noncommutative spaces. A key relationship between the deformed Fourier transform and its classical counterpart is identified, while an inverse deformed Fourier transform is successfully constructed. The study reveals that the deformed Fourier transform preserves certain quadratic forms analogous to their classical equivalents, which forms the basis for the development of deformed Weyl calculus. Formally, this new calculus enables an algebra of differential operators whose elements correspond to symbols under the algebra of functions, which forms the foundation for the representation of these operators as multiplication operators following a suitable commutative Gelfand-Naimark theorem. A noncommutative version of the stationary phase lemma is successfully constructed, which is essential for understanding the asymptotic behavior of functions within the envelope algebra. Formally, this lemma demonstrates that the algebra of differential operators is strongly deformed relative to its classical counterpart, which allows functions and operator representations to be associated with their classical counterparts via the asymptotic limit. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology.

In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 80 Gb/s over extended distances in a single mode fiber, which is a key requirement for resolving chromatic dispersion issues in data-intensive submarine cable systems that support multiple optical amplifiers. To accomplish this, 80Gb/s signals are generated using 4x200Gb/s continuous phase shift keying (CPSK) modules and amplified via Raman amplification, with the experiment showing a 5800km distance with acceptable signal quality (eye diagram) after transmission through a 580km demonstration loop. Although the results are initially achieved in a laboratory setting, they are scalable to multi-channel systems for future high-speed optical cable systems.

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution to capture long-term temporal dependencies. Despite being effective, optimizing their vast number of parameters and quantities of time-dilation factors can be challenging. This study introduces an innovative framework called Time-Dilated Convolution Factor Graph (TDCFG) that reuses dilated convolutional filters across different scales. By doing so, TDCFG significantly cuts the number of parameters and ensures optimal sharing of learned features across time scales. Notably, this framework demands only one less learnable parameter per input data point and outperforms standard TCNs in both accuracy and efficiency. Time-Dilated Convolution Factor Graph (TDCFG) achieves remarkable results on multiple datasets for speech recognition and time-series classification tasks.

This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency. Additionally, a corresponding statement is demonstrated for a broader class of varieties.

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for 2098 GeV $^ {208}$Pb+$^{208}$Pb collisions and various system sizes. The shape of the distribution of the difference between the angle and magnitude fluctuations is well described by a simple theoretical model, indicating that these fluctuations are primarily random in nature. Furthermore, the data reveals differences in the fluctuations between different experimental setups and from previously reported values of deterministic particle flow, which have been used to identify any reductions in the average values of particle flow angle and magnitude fluctuations as rapidity increases.

The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. Our theoretical framework involves populating data cells with possible values from a defined set, thereby creating a set of completed tables. Our objective is to ensure that at least one such table remains consistent. To accomplish this, we employ a logic-based methodology utilizing first-order language with classical truth values, where each statement corresponds to a specific dependency and is considered true for some consistent completed table. Given the challenge and complexity of determining if a statement is true in at least one such table, our work shifts focus to handling statements with a different property - being valid in at least one such table, thereby aligning with concepts of declarative specification and evaluation. A key aspect of this theory is interpreting statements as having truth values indicating their validity or inconsistency with respect to the original data table. This interpretation enables the assessment of data quality metrics and relational statements. Furthermore, we develop a method to compute these values based on the frequency of outcomes in the set of completed tables. Notably, this approach can also be applied to statements already valid in at least one such table, thereby offering a practical means to handle statements without forcing exclusion.

This study introduces a new dynamic econometric model count data, addressing the limitations of traditional time-invariant models. We propose a novel generalized autoregressive model with time-varying parameters and demonstrate its advantages through simulations and real-world applications. A consistent estimator of the model's fractional integration order is developed, along with implications for forecasting. Our findings include the establishment of asymptotic normality of the estimator and the development of an asymptotically accurate forecast confidence interval. We further provide an efficient non-Gaussian maximum likelihood estimation method for the model's parameters. The study's results are supported by the following key contributions: (i) detailed examination of forecasting performance, (ii) development of an efficient estimation method for the model's parameters, (iii) derivation of consistency for the estimator of the model's fractional integration order, and (iv) derivation of asymptotic normality of the estimator.

We have presented the initial results from the Tononzintla Project, which is centered on the globular cluster Tononzintla 2 (GCs2). Using the APO 2.5m telescope and the HIRES spectrograph, we obtained optical spectra for 18 stars within the cluster. These spectra allowed for the measurement of stellar parameters and chemical compositions. The data revealed that Tononzintla 2 shares several key characteristics with other well-studied Milky Way globular clusters. The clusters exhibit metallicity of [Fe/H] = -1.03 $\pm$ 0.07, a temperature range of T$_{eff}$ = 4600-5800 K, and similar values for surface gravity. Moreover, they possess [Al/Fe] = 0.13 $\pm$ 0.07, indicating a presence of nitrogen-enriched stars. The analysis of the clusters' stellar populations indicates the presence of an intermediate population of nitrogen-enriched stars, which is an area of further investigation. The composition of the clusters closely resembles that of some well-studied metallicity similar globular clusters. The Isabelle Archive, a comprehensive collection of formal proofs spanning over ten years of development, has accumulated more than ten gigabytes of content in its HTML presentation. The size and diversity of these proofs have posed significant obstacles in making the material easily accessible and comprehensible to a wider audience. To address these challenges, we have created IsarBook, an extension to the Isar language that facilitates the creation of thematically organized and visually appealing books and websites. By leveraging IsarBook's features, such as side margins, cross-references, and a unified syntax for mathematical expressions, we have been able to produce polished materials like the "HOL-Library" library and the IsarReference manual, which serve as prime examples of this approach in action. These projects now incorporate more than three thousand pages of content and have achieved a cohesive presentation, which was previously unattainable with the Archive's standard format. The new IsarBook syntax allows for enhanced presentation of definitions, theorems, and other content, resulting in a consistent and visually appealing output. The improved features of IsarBook, combined with the archival capabilities of the Isabelle Archive, offer a new and effective way to share formal proofs with a broader audience.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously reported a narrower range of 1.14 to 1.23 without the leading logarithmic corrections, and incorporating these corrections, we have refined the estimate to 1.196, which aligns with Monte Carlo simulation findings.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem. Furthermore, we determined a threshold for this convexity barrier, showing that it coincides with the threshold for the algorithm's performance, even in a high-dimensional setting. Notably, this result provides the first instance of a theory connecting the optimization landscape to the algorithm's performance, including the AMP, beyond problems with a convex function.

The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization theorem for smooth vector fields with a full set of nearby first integrals, especially those at nondegenerate singular points. This theoretical validation relies heavily on key concepts, including the formal orbital linearization theorem for formally integrable vector fields, the application of the blowing-up technique, and the application of the Sternberg-Chen theorem regarding formally equivalent smooth hyperbolic vector fields.

This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can efficiently model the electron
correlation potential of atoms with multiple electrons. Training an anti-Hartree
Fock loss function with eCPNN yields accurate one-electron wavefunctions, which
effectively represent the exact electron density and demonstrate remarkable
generalization abilities. Notably, the trained models excel at extrapolating to
previously untrained atomic configurations without retraining, when applied to
homologous systems. Furthermore, the system shows exceptional performance in
intrinsically challenging systems such as anomalous ions like He+.

We have identified a massive structure, dubbed the Giant Arc, which spans approximately 300 megaparsecs and lies directly behind the Sh2 208 nebula at the galactic center. The detection of this massive structure, along with 11 other similar instances out of 164 observed, is inconsistent with the standard cosmological model's predictions, suggesting the need for a revised theoretical framework. Combining gravitational redshift data with optical imaging of the Giant Arc, we determined its spatial extent to be around 10 megaparsecs in height and 300 megaparsecs in length, located at a depth of z=0.06. The formation of such an arc-shaped structure poses a challenge to our current understanding of cosmology, as it is unlikely to be a product of structure collapse within the $\Lambda$CDM model. We propose alternative hypotheses, including the existence of massive, filamentary structures within our cosmic neighborhood, or the influence of a massive, nearby structure on our perception of the local universe.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration. This study showcases a method to extract aerosol depth from such data, employing a forward model that simulates observations based on assumed values for aerosol properties and accounts for instrumental effects. An iterative process uses this model to determine the most likely properties from actual measurements, validated with both artificial data and real observational data from various locations and systems over multiple seasons. The analysis revealed a correlation between the aerosol depth and a related metric, with the method demonstrating the ability to track seasonal variations in aerosol properties at different sites. Although the system's absolute calibration influences the absolute values of the aerosul properties, the relative variations are accurate, and the determined properties align with existing scientific data within the margin of error.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using convolutional neural networks has seen significant advancement. Current methods, categorized into template matching and regression approaches, focus on local image features to determine object pose. In this research, we explore an alternative strategy using global graph representations, which involves learning both node and edge features within the context of a template graph. This approach allows for a rigid object pose to be accurately represented. To handle viewpoint and illumination inconsistencies, we introduce a re-identification process to match the detection query with the most relevant registered object. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, particularly in complex scenarios involving multiple objects of the same type. The code is available at https://github.com/HaiguangLi/GlobalObjectPoseEstimation.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, due to their ability to model and track discontinuities, such as cracks, within linear and nonlinear materials. Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its difficulties in conserving momentum and limited ability to model corners, has remained the most extensively researched approach. In this study, we enhance the bond-based Peridynamic model by incorporating a novel kernel that represents not only the distances between material points but also their angles, effectively increasing the amount of geometric information considered. The modified approach successfully demonstrates improved momentum conservation, easier modeling of stress concentrations, and more precise simulation of dislocations. Furthermore, the model's performance has been validated using numerical simulations and real-world experiments, demonstrating its ability to accurately simulate and track defects in materials like copper and polycrystalline nanogold.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparse precision matrix from potentially dependent samples and even
from multiple related datasets. The GGLasso scheme can be extended to high-dimensional
data where the number of features surpasses the number of samples. GGLasso employs
the Frank-Wolfe and Coordinate Descent algorithms to efficiently solve these problems.
It includes implementations of both the basic and multi-dataset Graphical Lasso
models. The package is easily customizable, featuring various statistical
metrics for model evaluation. GGLasso is suitable for applications such as
feature selection in high-dimensional data, covariance estimation, and estimating
the number of relevant features.

Numerous numerical methods for biomolecules have been developed over the last few decades, all aiming to resolve time-dependent processes within these complex molecules through classical mechanics. Building upon this foundation, we extend these methods to address the issue of calculating configurational averages in biomolecules interacting with a surrounding solvent, treated as an integrable quantum system. We demonstrate that certain numerical methods retain high accuracy and efficiency when used in combination with a quantum dynamics approach for calculating the average. These methods retain their reliability and efficiency across a broader range of solvent conditions due to the application of the real-time path integral formalism, resulting in the generation of a weighted ensemble that remains valid over time. Furthermore, we establish that the required sampling can be achieved with significantly fewer grid points than typically required in propagator-based methods, such as the real-time path integral propagator (RPIM) or the real-time configuration interaction (RCI), due to the utilization of the Heisenberg representation. With these advancements, we are able to accurately and efficiently model larger systems and include essential anharmonic effects, overcoming limitations previously encountered in RPIM and RCI methods.

Numerical relativity simulations, incorporating Wigner functions for dark matter with masses up to 10 times those of the binary black holes, reveal consistent behavior in wave dark matter across this range. This observation is reconciled by formulating a dimensionless parameter that captures the relative masses of the dark matter and black holes. This parameter reveals that the apparent uniformity in the behavior of wave dark matter is governed by a phase transition at a critical value. Below this value, corresponding to an infinite mass limit, black hole dynamics dominate. However, values exceeding this critical point reflect the behavior of an infinite-mass binary. A precise formula, derived in this study, accurately predicts this critical value. Additionally, mergers distort the effective potential, potentially causing a temporary increase in the gravitational wave frequency. This could lead to the emergence of overtones that might offer insights into the mass of wave dark matter. Furthermore, mergers can generate secondary gravitational waves, potentially observable as peaks in the frequency spectrum. These findings could have implications for the detection of wave dark matter through gravitational waves.

We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with rotating endpoints. Three distinct boundary condition types are examined, and it is demonstrated that all share a common structural property. Furthermore, we derive an approximate stability decay rate for two of these conditions, while the third is handled separately, along with a specific stability estimate. A key factor influencing stability across all cases is identified and given a geometric interpretation. This interpretation enables us to predict which configurations lead to unstable systems.

Researchers utilized computer simulations to analyze the effects of lens materials, such as PMMA and Stycast 1090SI, on the detection of aluminum defects using ultrasound. They also examined how changes in gel material influenced the reflections within the lens and the resulting impact on detecting flaws within the metal target. To minimize the complexities introduced by the air gap between the sample and lens, a comparative analysis was conducted along with an assessment of the lens's ability to detect flaws in various forms. Furthermore, a data basis was created to quantify the changes introduced by the lens and understanding of the resulting effect on defect detection sensitivity was gained.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. We have used various multi-layer networks to test and demonstrate our approach, including a description-based model that simulates how information spreads across different network layers over time.

We tackle the issue of non-Gaussian image degradation and algorithmic-induced distortions on high-quality images, addressing them on images directly taken from cameras. To tackle this problem, we propose a novel two-branch architecture featuring an image-to-image translation module and a discriminative assessment unit. Notably, our model eschews the need for Gaussian noise injection and synthetic image processing, by training an auxiliary branch to evaluate both real and generated images. Notably, our approach involves introducing controlled noise during training, aligning with the camera's inherent noise patterns. Experimental results showcase the model's efficacy in handling diverse image degradation types, showcasing superior performance compared to other methods. Additionally, the approach demonstrates the feasibility of direct camera-to-display image presentation, with enhanced visual quality.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a deformed GL(4,R) transformation that represents a de Sitter spacetime. 
By applying the standard lightcone gauge to the de Sitter spacetime, we obtain the 
anti-lightcone gauge for the generated $R$-Poincar\'e algebra. The purpose of this 
study is to introduce a non-linear Poincar\'e algebra in the lightcone gauge and 
subsequently generate de Sitter spacetime through the inverse Fock coordinate 
transformation. We demonstrate that specific choice of deformation parameters in 
the generated $R$-Poincar\'e algebra achieves this, as the inverse Fock transformation 
becomes the standard lightcone-to-anti-lightcone map in the spacetime.

This study introduces an open source Python framework that utilizes background knowledge and observational data for the purpose of inferring causal relationships. This framework is comprised of the 'cdt' package, which executes a comprehensive causal discovery process to produce a directed Causal Network. The framework is designed to accommodate various input types including interventional and experimental data, and it incorporates established methods including TAILOR and the RXR approach. Researchers can utilize the framework to explore and compare the effects of multiple causal models, and it is suitable for integration into existing machine learning pipelines due to its support for various causal models and return models.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the surface seal formation that occurs when the sphere's velocity is not high enough to create an air cavity. Observations were made directly, using high-speed cameras to track the water around the sphere in a two-dimensional setup. The research shows that the time it takes for the surface seal to break is linearly related to the inverse of the impact velocity for spheres with a Kraus number less than one. A distinct pattern of water flow emerges around spheres with a diameter of less than one millimeter in this phase. The article also outlines the characteristics of an intermediate regime between the surface seal and the air cavity creation.

A recent discovery by Bartsch, Hachmann, Rapp, and Schenkel revealed that localized global anomalies in higher-dimensional bulk theories are effectively equivalent to non-trivial boundary terms in certain symmetry invariant theta-terms. Building on this, we establish a link between these anomaly-cancelling terms and terms in low-dimensional effective field theories (EFTs). Specifically, we show that EFTs constructed from given bulk anomalies always incorporate the necessary theta-terms as anomaly extensions. These additional EFT symmetry invariant theta-terms correspond to the anomalous effective action of the reduced DFT after integrating out the original anomaly-free DFT. We argue that Wess-Zumino terms can be reinterpreted as generalized theta-terms and investigate the impact of adding Wess-Zumino terms to an EFT in relation to its parent deep learning theory (EFT).

Mobile devices are increasingly using multiple separate hardware areas to improve overall performance and user experience. This architectural shift offers the potential to significantly enhance user trust and security in critical applications. One such application is secure voting on mobile devices, involving multiple separate hardware areas. This process involves casting votes on mobile devices within a specific context. We present the concept of blockchain-enabled mobile voting, utilizing a consortium blockchain approach and a novel design called VotBlock. This system employs a cloud broker to manage VotBlock's operation, ensuring the mobility and confidentiality of the voting process. The security of both privileged and non-privileged users is guaranteed through the system's design. Our assessment of the implementation using the Intel SoC FPGA confirms the feasibility and robust security of this approach.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards, a scenario that fundamentally differs from traditional reinforcement learning with fixed corrupted rewards. The corruption rates in both cases differ significantly, and the reward corruptions are bounded within $[-r_{\max}, r_{\max}]$. We developed a robust policy learning algorithm based on the Policy Gradient method, utilizing the UCB2 technique to manage the adversially corrupted rewards. Theoretical analysis shows that this algorithm finds an $\varepsilon$-optimality policy within $T = O\left(\frac{s^2 r_{\max}^2}{\varepsilon^2} \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon} + \frac{s^2 r_{\max}^2 A}{\varepsilon^2} \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)$ rounds, where $s$ and $A$ denote the number of states and actions, respectively, and $r_{\max}$ represents the $\varepsilon$-optimality value. Notably, the $\varepsilon$-optimality is directly influenced by $r_{\max}$, the maximum range of the corrupted rewards.

We uncover an unselectable version of the box game paradox, featuring players making remarkably accurate predictions of unknown real numbers without access to relevant information. Additionally, our analysis confirms the requirement of choice in the resolving solution.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics and information science is centered on the use of dark quantum states in semiconductor quantum dots.  These "dark" states, including dark excitons and optical Fock states, offer significant advantages over "bright" excitons and quantum emitters with quantum numbers, due to their inherent non-Abelian properties which facilitate efficient quantum gate operations. A novel technique, involving the application of a quantum dot to a parabolic potential to create an "artificial atom," enhances the stability and accessibility of dark states by shifting them to higher energy levels. This method allows for the realization of a dark quantum state with dark excitons within a two-dimensional quantum well using a gate, resulting in a 10-fold increase in lifetime and dominant population of dark states (exceeding 90%). The high proportion of dark states in this system is particularly notable, as it surpasses the typical 10% seen in other dark emulators. The observed phenomenon is driven by a shift in the energy levels of dark and bright excitons, as well as the Landau levels of the electron gas, leading to a pronounced increase in the energy of the dark exciton relative to the bright exciton. The outcome is the dominant population of a dark state with a long lifetime of approximately 1 ns, in contrast to a bright exciton lifetime of around 300 ps. This research marks a milestone in the field, as it is among the first demonstrations of a dark quantum state

Our investigation into a 2D electronic lattice structure reveals self-similar fractal patterns within the band structure of the Moore–Read lattice. By incorporating hole pockets into the valuce band and analyzing their scattering with electrons, we establish the existence of Dirac cones within this lattice. Notably, the fractal nature of the band structure arises without requiring a magnetic field.

Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters and photon detectors. Despite catalysis, no extra photons are added to these states. Both the quantum properties and classical analogues of SPCCSs exhibit exceptional behavior. Notably, they display profound quantum effects, including single-photon superoscillations, robust anti-bunching, intense quantum interference, and robust Fock-state factorizations, all stemming from coherent-state catalysis. SPCCSs are highly suitable for quantum information applications, particularly in quantum communication and computing. An efficient classical simulation algorithm has been devised to analyze the SPCCSs' intricate features and verify their distinctive characteristics.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space into complex self-dual gravitational fields in four-dimensional Minkowski space. We delve into the properties of null and non-null bivectors in flat spacetime and provide explicit examples of both types within the context of the pp-waves in the standard form $ds^2=2du(dv+a(u)A_ia_i du^2+ A_iA_i du^2)$.

A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure.

This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to a blood coagulation problem. Notably, we examine the possibility of estimating unknown parameters within model equations, demonstrating how the proposed framework can be applied in this context.

A significant difficulty in the clinical diagnosis of esophageal cancer lies in the laborious task of marking tumors on CT scans. Previous research has explored various techniques to assist with this difficult delineation. Our proposed approach leverages prior knowledge from healthy CT scans to enhance tumor segmentation. To achieve this, we train a conditional generative model called Cycle Conditional Generative Adversarial Network to generate images of apparent CT scans by applying a tumor mask to normal scans. These artificially produced images are then used as supplementary training data for a binary segmentation model. Our proposed method yielded superior results compared to other existing methods, as evidenced by evaluations conducted by radiation oncologists.

The expense of drilling offshore wells is significantly elevated, necessitating precise well placement within the target reservoir to minimize costs. Achieving accurate positioning is facilitated through real-time imaging of the wellbore and reservoir boundaries during drilling, using advanced image processing to determine the well's spatial location. However, existing methods solely focus on visual data, disregarding the geologist's input. These experts possess valuable insights into the geological formations, rock types, and their distribution patterns in the area, which can be mapped as probabilistic maps of subsurface features. By integrating these maps with the well's surface trajectory, the decision-making process for navigating the well through the target reservoir is automated, thereby reducing the high operational costs associated with offshore wells. Our proposed approach achieves this by combining computer vision and geosteering techniques through a deep learning framework that learns the distribution of geological features and predicts the reservoir boundaries during drilling, resulting in improved boundary predictions compared to baseline methods and validated through a real-world field case study.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that is complicated by the nested nature of certain entities, which pose challenges to the development of effective solutions. In this paper, we introduce a holistic NER framework that utilizes bidirectional transformations to extract nested entities from each other rather than independently, without resorting to heuristic post-processing methods. By formulating the n-ary relationship extraction (REL) task as bidirectional sequence-to-sequence (B2S2S) transitions, we achieve a unified approach for nested NER, sequence to tree (S2T) generation, and n-ary REL that allows for mutual reinforcement of the derived trees. To validate the effectiveness of our B2S2S framework, we create high-quality nested NER and S2T datasets, and conduct thorough experiments demonstrating superior performance compared to existing models. Our results show that the B2S2S framework achieves the most competitive results in both nested NER and S2T datasets, and the generated holistic trees exhibit high quality with low error rates.

We extend the use of tropical methods to counting in arithmetic problems, such as enumerating objects in higher-dimensional spaces over global fields. By applying valuation theory and studying reductions of equations over local fields, we show that equations for plane sextics with tangent lines at infinity can be reduced to simpler forms. This allows us to connect the number of ways certain tropical bitangents appear multiple times to a specific set of tangency points. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between certain tropical bitangents and a specific set of edges in a tropical curve, providing a practical way to calculate a tangent point and verify its accuracy through numerical experiments.

Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The objective of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, the method achieves a comparable level of accuracy.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require a new standard set of high-quality data for both the training and evaluation of these systems.

Tantalum oxide nanoparticles, specifically $\mathrm{Ta}_2\mathrm{O}_5$, $\mathrm{TaOCl}_5$, and $\mathrm{TaOCl}_3$, have the potential to be effective hadronotherapy agents for cancer treatment using proton therapy. To assess their suitability, researchers are examining how these nanoparticles interact with incident protons. Additionally, the biocompatibility of these materials and the possibility of incorporating the oxide into radioopaque dental fillings, which contain non-degradable metallic components, are being considered. To address the complexity of modeling dielectric materials in Monte Carlo simulations, a parameterization method is used to represent the materials' dielectric properties. The resulting energy loss functions are computed and compared to existing models, termed "berg" and "hira", as well as experimental data. The oxide parameterization is incorporated into the Geant4 Monte Carlo simulation framework, and the results show a closer alignment with empirical data, indicating an improvement in the simulation accuracy of energy loss in dielectric materials. To further validate the findings, the simulated data is compared with experimental data, demonstrating a closer match when using the oxide parameterization. The researchers are planning to conduct more comprehensive comparisons with the "berg" and "hira" models in upcoming studies.

Previous studies have linked microblogging activity to population density, economic activity, and other socioeconomic factors in various regions. This research took a different approach by examining how regions influence each other through the circulation of information, including both accurate and misleading content on Weibo. It did so by measuring the impact of local economic activity and a non-economic factor (the prevalence of certain personality traits within each region) on cross-regional information circulation. This approach allowed for the estimation of information "depth" for each region and its effect on cross-regional information circulation. Notably, it discovered that areas with higher levels of neuroticism and regions with low levels of openness had a greater influence on cross-regional information circulation, especially when considering a lag effect. This implies that the circulation of content, including misinformation, on Weibo may be affected by the personality traits of individuals within each region.

We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called SUSIE, a semi-supervised method that leverages labeled and unlabeled data to identify anomalies in real-time data streams. Lateral thinking attacks, a groundbreaking concept, demonstrate the effectiveness of LLMs in creating these challenging scenarios, which involve using AI to mimic the behavior of genuine users in real-time data streams. In our comprehensive study, we show that LLM-based methods using these techniques are highly challenging to detect, outperforming the current state-of-the-art in the field. On the other hand, we discovered that traditional supervised learning algorithms used in the CDXs scenario are highly effective in detecting these lateral thinking attacks, even though they are quite straightforward. In contrast, the SUSIE detection method, the only method to successfully detect lateral thinking attacks in the CDXs scenario, has limited practical applicability due to significant computational constraints. The SUSIE detection method is the first to detect these attacks, but it is not feasible in a production environment as the only method to successfully detect lateral thinking attacks in the CDXs scenario, but it is not feasible in a production environment due to significant computational constraints.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods.

Building on previous work, we propose an algorithm to randomly generate ordered trees of any degree, based on a pre-specified sequence of numbers representing possible node connections. Our method allows for the generation of binary, n-ary trees, or those with various connection patterns. We demonstrate that this algorithm is both accurate and efficient, running in O(n) time with 'n' representing the number of desired nodes. Additionally, we explore potential applications of the method in problem reduction techniques used by computational mathematicians.

Quantum field theory complexity is particularly challenging to define and measure due to its vast number of degrees of freedom. A promising approach to address this issue is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions. By combining the concepts of simple operator bases from CFT and the use of variational circuits from quantum information, a specific definition of operator complexity is established. This framework is then applied to calculate the complexity of fundamental CFT operators, including single and multi-operator perturbations of the energy density, as well as the complexity growth following an quantum quench. Notably, this study demonstrates that the resulting time evolution of complexity mirrors that of a system starting with a local disturbance and entering its unitary time development.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances.

The study utilizes a sophisticated statistical method to estimate the uncertainty associated with detecting a yet-unknown planet, similar to that in a recent research paper. The effectiveness of this approach is tested using data on solar system planets and the potential for finding "Planet X" is analyzed in terms of distance, brightness, and uncertainty, with specific considerations for how the measurement uncertainties change based on the distance variable. The current data shows that measuring Planet X with a heliocentric distance of less than 800 AU can be achieved with less than 20 percent uncertainty using existing telescopes, while more precise measurements become unfeasible at greater distances due to the increasing uncertainty. The data further supports the validity of restricting the dataset to less than 800 AU due to the FPP's 95 percent credible interval falling within this range. The research implies that the current data can be analyzed without introducing an upper limit on heliocentric distance as it automatically falls within 750 AU at 68 percent and 900 AU at 95 percent.

Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages. Initially, it enables automatic TM expansion by incorporating monolingual data and eliminating the need for parallelization. Secondly, it enables the retrieval of relevant, contextually similar memories with contrasting meanings, thereby mitigating the risk of copying incorrect translations. We conducted comprehensive experiments to evaluate the translation quality, TM precision, and recall. The results indicate that our framework yields superior performance compared to standard TM exploitation methods and achieves a 5 points increase in BLEORs on the WMT 2016 English to German translation task.

Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later removed, and upon re-examination, we found no statistically significant evidence supporting the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Our analysis does indicate the presence of local non-Gaussian fluctuations in the CMB, suggesting that the real sky may differ from theoretical predictions.

This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which involved introducing a Yamabe flow based on fractional curvature and demonstrating the existence of mild solutions. The current research expands on that study by establishing the convergence of the flow under certain data conditions within a broader framework. The new results are derived from an approach simplified by Struwe in his book.

To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for calculating prototypes often struggle due to the influence of outliers. This research proposes a new, effective framework that utilizes an episodic prototype generator to create more representative prototypes from limited support data, reducing the impact of outliers and resulting in superior performance. The framework's validity is confirmed through extensive experiments on standard evaluation datasets, indicating its versatility and efficiency when compared to other competitive methods that include traditional mean pooling, EOS, and EOSQ approaches, showing significant performance gains particularly in tasks with small sample sizes and across different classification tasks in the mini ImageNet dataset.

Cross-domain recommendation is gaining significant attention in recent years as it tackles the issues of cold-start and sparseness associated with single-domain recommendations. However, existing approaches often fail to account for multiple sparse domains simultaneously, treating them as independent entities without recognizing their inherent diversity. In contrast, we propose the Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) model, a novel method that embraces the varied preferences of each domain by allowing them to be represented as distinct entities. By doing so, our model promotes collaboration among sparse domains, effectively overcoming the limitations of traditional cross-domain and multi-domain recommendation models. Notably, the entity-based architecture of MSDCR enables a seamless integration with rich auxiliary information, such as user and item attributes, item content, and domain names. As a result, our model achieves a seamless synergy between collaborative filtering and deep learning, ultimately delivering superior performance in terms of recommendation accuracy. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our model, showcasing significant advancements over existing models.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context are subsets of ℝ^𝒹 with intrinsic geometric properties, evident in examples like the second-order cone, semi-algebraic cones, and polyhedral cones. These cones are prevalent in structural engineering, material science, and other fields, yet they are rarely incorporated into current interior point solvers. We introduce BooleansCones, a pioneering library of exotic cones tailored for use in convex optimization, featuring efficient implementations of numerous specialized cones and operations to merge, intersect, and transform these cones. Experiments demonstrate the benefits of utilizing these exotic cones in IPM solvers, especially when compared to the issues that arise from representing these cones using standard component-wise constraints. In these scenarios, IPM solvers can achieve levels of efficiency and numerical stability comparable to native cone implementations, even for problems with extremely high dimensions.

The success of automated quality control in medical image analysis depends heavily on the development of an effective evaluation system. This system must be able to monitor the accuracy and consistency of the primary AI model's output. To enable this, we established a comprehensive framework for our Quality Control (QC) system, which leverages ensemble-based segmentation and incorporates a comprehensive dataset comprising 1200 MRI brain scans. We found that the QC system's performance is influenced by the type of ensemble method employed, the diversity within the input dataset, and the inclusion of both hard and easy cases. Our comparative analysis of multiple baseline models revealed the value of a carefully selected MRI inference model in enhancing the QC system's effectiveness. The results we obtained provide a reference framework for the intricate process of QC in medical image analysis. To fully appreciate our findings, supplementary video materials are included, presenting vivid visual examples of the QC system's capabilities.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm. Numerical analysis of a test power network revealed the effectiveness of our approach and the potential impact of private EVs on improving grid resilience. Furthermore, we demonstrated how central coordination can lead to efficient outcomes comparable to decentralized decision-making.

Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) offers an cost-effective alternative to DRAM with extended data persistence. In comparison to traditional DRAM, Optane DC PMMs are slower but can be replaced without data loss. While Optane DC PMMs support load and store operations for atomic replacements, the more common comparison to DRAM involves sorting non-decreasing memory access patterns. We developed and evaluated three distinct Optane DC PMM memory access simulation methods, with the most advanced sequence simulation method showing up to 2.07x speedup and 1.71x energy efficiency improvement over the existing state-of-the-art, as demonstrated in an extensive evaluation on the Intel Xeon E5-2650 processor.

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We found that all studied compounds possess an anti-skubitts crystal structure and demonstrate metallic behavior. Specifically, GdSn3 and the GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds show a paramagnetic state, while CmSn3 exhibits a ferromagnetic state with a total magnetic moment of 4.27 $\mu_B$. The magnetic moment in CmSn3 is entirely contributed by the 5f electrons of Cm. The magnetic moment in the CmSn3 lattice is localized at the Cm site and nearly absent in the Sn sublattice. The magnetic moment in the GdSn3 and GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds is primarily 5d electron based and occurs in the Gd site. The projected density of states and charge distribution further validate our findings. The minimum convex hull analysis shows the stability of all compounds in the anti-skubitts structure. The phonon dispersion curves confirm the dynamic stability of the compounds within this structural framework. The density of states and projected density of states provide additional insights to support our findings.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the Standard Model, known as the bilepton model, which involves changing the gauge group to $SU(2)_R \otimes SU(2)_L \otimes U(1)_{B-R}$. It discusses how adding specific bileptons affects the gauge couplings and the mass parameters of the model. Potential experimental evidence for this model can be found in various tests, including weight distributions in proton collisions, decay patterns of the model's new $Z_R$ boson, and the decay of the model's $Z_L$ partner.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. H. Hughes demonstrated in 1964 that OGS is equivalent to the unique factorization property when increasing consecutive generator exponents are permitted only once. Building on this, our study examines the representation of individual group elements as the product of non-repeating squares of generators from Sn, also in the context of ordered generating sequences.

Utilizing the Pantheon supernova sample and its associated redshift data, we examined the impact of weak lensing due to dark matter halos on the observed brightness of Type Ia supernovae. A statistical analysis was conducted to estimate the lensing effect within the confidence range of the measurements, excluding the lensing impact from dark matter halos. Furthermore, we explored the implications of weak lensing on the estimation of the Hubble constant ($H_0$) and found a strong correlation between the observed brightness of supernovae and the lensing effect at redshifts greater than 0.15, with a quantifiable coefficient of determination. This discovery may aid in distinguishing the lensing impact from the unknown intrinsic variations in Type Ia supernovae, particularly when estimating $H_0$.

These are lecture notes for a 6-hour mini-course on stochastic partial differential equations presented at the University of Oxford in April-May 2021. 

The main objective of these lecture notes is to provide an in-depth explanation of the variational method for monotone and coercive stochastic partial differential equations. 

The necessary background on Hilbert space-based functional analysis, operator theory, and stochastic analysis has been recapitulated within the lecture notes and further relevant references are included. 

The concluding chapter covers the pathwise approach.

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will require reliable links between photons and electronic or nuclear spins. In silicon, T-type damage centers have shown great potential as a result of mechanical stress, creating unique properties through a state of degeneracy. However, a deeper understanding of their characteristics and a method for dictating their configuration are still needed. We have achieved a fine assessment of the damage center's electronic state using two-color pump-probe spectroscopy and polarization-resolved techniques, supported by supported semi-empirical modeling. Our study has provided a detailed description of the damage center's characteristics and demonstrated increased sensitivity to stress and temperature, along with the identification of stress-induced splitting in degenerate states. These findings provide important direction for utilizing T centers in photon-spin interfaces and a new approach for tuning the charge state of these centers.

MRI technology utilizes radio waves to scan the human body and obtain precise, pain-free diagnostic images. These images enable radiologists to visually assess anatomy and physiological processes within the body, ultimately facilitating early disease diagnosis and treatment. Advanced imaging capabilities, combined with sophisticated processing techniques, enable detection of hard-to-spot tumors. This assignment delves into Automated Tumor Detection by comparing conventional image processing methods, such as morphological analysis and regional growth algorithms, in order to explore their application and effectiveness.

This research paper introduces a novel algebraic variant of the degenerate Bernoulli polynomial, along with associated algebraic variant degenerate Bernoulli numbers. We examine key properties of this new polynomial, including algebraic variant degenerate Bernoulli-type numbers, relationships with degenerate Faulhaber's formula, and connections to ordinary Bernoulli polynomials. proofs of the seen properties of this new polynomial, including its recursive formula, and let $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$ be a parameter.

The high activity levels of M dwarfs, caused by their significant stellar spots, pose a challenge in identifying potential exoplanets. To overcome this issue, researchers aim to develop a method for spot detection that accounts for the complex relationship between stellar activity and X-ray or ultraviolet emissions. A new approach to this problem is introduced, which utilizes a machine learning algorithm to detect and classify stars in X-rays and ultraviolet spectra, thereby revealing the presence of stellar spots. The study employs this approach to compare data from two datasets: one collected during a period of high stellar activity and another during a period of low activity. By analyzing the differences in the algorithm's output, a spectral difference map is generated that highlights the characteristics of stellar spots. Furthermore, a newly introduced metric, which measures the likelihood of spot presence based on the algorithm's classification, allows for a distinction between periods of high and low activity without a labeled dataset. This approach also reveals the ability to detect periods of activity and potentially uncover the characteristics of stellar spots.

This paper proposes a pair of methods for designing efficient and scalable strategies in Wireless Sensor Networks, specifically addressing Link Quality Estimation and Route Discovery. Firstly, an estimate of link functionality is determined by comparing packet acknowledgments, and subsequently, a link quality estimate is generated using a mathematical formula. Notably, our link assessment method operates without consuming additional network resources and generates results within a single acknowledgment transmission time. We developed two route discovery protocols, distributed and hierarchical in nature, utilizing link quality estimates to identify optimal routes. A key feature of these protocols is their ability to embed route information within existing acknowledgment packets, eliminating the need for separate messages for route advertisement. Overall, our evaluation indicates satisfactory performance in terms of energy efficiency, packet delivery success, control message overhead, and route calculation time.

Different object detectors utilize scene context in various ways, leading us to
categorize them into those that use ego-vehicle context, individual object
features, and the relationships between objects. To effectively test the effect
of object context on both the unconnected and dependent objects, we first
classify common objects into three categories: typical, unique, and rare, and
then employ a broad range of object detectors for our experiments. We found on
average that on typical objects, a high-performing two-stage object detector
produces true positives with accurate Ego-vehicle context but over-segmentation
issues. It also yields more true positives compared to object segmentation tools.
However, when dealing with unique objects, the detector fails to make use of
the object context, resulting in inaccurate segmentation. In contrast, when
encountering rare objects, a majority of objects prove to be both rare and
uncommon in the dataset, prompting us to modify our approach by using a rare
object that is prominent in the scene and common in the database. Under these
circumstances, the object detector, being an effective feature extractor,
produces precise masks. Nevertheless, performance drops when employing less
common objects, both unique and rare, in the test images. To address this shortcoming, we proposed two external modules that enable a basic object detector to
