For nearly 60 years, researchers have been searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through SETI initiatives, with a Dyson Sphere as a potential detectable indicator of advanced civilizations. A Dyson Sphere is an artificial mega-structure capable of harnessing a star's complete energy output and could signify a highly developed alien society. In this context, we investigate the feasibility of using a black hole Dyson Sphere to power an Earth-like planet, specifically exploring the possibility of such a structure enabling the observation of distant galaxies with a telescope. By applying general relativistic principles, we determine the energy output and visual appearance of this mega-structure, finding that its total power could exceed 10^56 erg/s, while an observer on its surface would perceive its star as having significantly altered stellar parameters. Although such a Dyson Sphere could enable the galaxy-wide detection of advanced civilizations, it would remain undetectable through traditional astronomical means from within its own galaxy.

Network-based services are vital for the financial stability of service providers, who must adhere to agreed-upon performance standards, or SLAs. To meet these standards, a network operator must have sufficient resources, which they can also use for revenue-generating purposes. In seeking to balance SLAs compliance and resource efficiency, operators face an optimal control challenge. This study formulates a stochastic dynamic programming approach to manage a dynamic resource allocation system, where the flow of resources is regulated by switching mechanisms. A key finding is that there exists an efficient switching mechanism to optimize SLAs compliance while minimizing excess resource accumulation. This mechanism can be simplified into a threshold-based switching mechanism, as proven in the context of an isolated system. Furthermore, a practical resource management strategy is developed, incorporating compliance cost minimization, based on the form of over-provisioning that characterizes efficient supply. This study also establishes an ergodicity property for the resulting system, indicating that, given a limited supply of excess resources, the system will consistently meet SLAs over time.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators, limiting the maximum beam current for those operating in transverse mode. This effect was first observed in 1946 at the Bevatron. As continuous beam sources become more prevalent in next-generation accelerators, the issue of beam breakup grows increasingly significant. This issue was initially studied at the DC accelerator DCDC in 1967, but the reported results were not fully reliable. We have re-examined beam breakup in DCDC, and our findings align well with theoretical predictions for both narrow and wide beam widths. This validation enables us to derive a reliable expression for the voltage profile of the DCDC kicker magnet's gap.

To determine the oscillation parameters in future neutrino experiments with high precision, sophisticated detectors known as near and far detectors are utilized to measure neutrino interactions accurately. These detectors rely on target volumes composed of scintillator trackers in three dimensions, which serve as crucial components in neutrino oscillation studies. Neutrino beams, specifically those produced using wide-angle sources, can cause the scintillator trackers to experience significant backgrounds from neutrino-induced reactions and secondary neutrinos. This study simulates low-energy $\bar{\nu}_\mu$ and $\nu_\mu$ interactions and secondary neutrino-induced reactions on the LAr-PC38 detector for the DUNE near detector plane, in order to assess the cross section uncertainties, systematic errors, and the absolute rates of these events.

A new variant of the discrete element method (DEM) is introduced to model the interactions between particles containing a thin film of water on their boundaries. The modifications to the model account for adhesive and viscous effects, with parameters set to represent conditions during the early stages of the solar nebula. Varying temperatures demonstrate that the presence of water significantly impacts particle interactions, with sticking probabilities on chondritic grains being highly temperature-dependent. Viscous dissipation leads to a decrease in sticking forces as temperature rises, resulting in sticking forces on water-covered particles being 10 to 1000 times greater than on dry particles near the nebula's hot center. The outcomes of the simulations suggest that the nebula may have been divided into regions of particle aggregation and granular flow due to these temperature effects. The results of the study have implications for the development of multi-scale DEM models and change existing assumptions incorporated into such simulations.

Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies like Kernel Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Semi-Supervised Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis. The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggfortify in ggplot2) graphical tools.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and intuitive nature. However, current methods struggle to effectively handle complex joint-space movements, which are essential for robots navigating unstructured environments. To address this limitation, a new cluster-based imitation learning approach is proposed, which uses extended kernelized movement primitives to efficiently represent and execute intricate motions. By incorporating extended kernel kernels, the method achieves superior approximation of high-dimensional target trajectories while simultaneously reducing unnecessary movements. Additionally, an optimized distance measure is developed to find similar motion patterns in the cluster network, and a new combination strategy is used to handle diverse motion primitives for accurate trajectory execution. The proposed approach is shown to outperform current state-of-the-art methods in terms of trajectory accuracy and end-effector movement efficiency.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit. This process involves evaluating a six-point amplitude in N=4 SYM under the NMRK configuration, where the rapidity gap between two central gluons is significantly narrower than the gaps between them and the outer gluons, which are in a collinear arrangement. By leveraging a six-to-four soft function approach, the CEV for two gluons can be related to the impact of shrinking two gluons in the rapidity domain, which is equivalent to taking the soft limit where their energy approaches zero. Under the NMRK limit, this amplitude decomposes into four soft functions parameterized by the rapidity gaps between the four pairs of collinear gluons. The factorization of the amplitude into hard, semi-hard, and soft functions within the NMRK limit was verified, and the results show consistency with both, the five-gluon amplitude and the CEV for two gluons in N=4 SYM within the appropriate kinematic limits.

A new class of superconductors emerges in very thin layers of materials like Lithium on top of ferroelectrics, characterized by high sensitivity to external magnetic fields due to Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Our analysis reveals that when a Zeeman magnetic field is applied, these Rashba and spin-split bands can combine in the presence of strong electron-phonon coupling, enabling superconductivity despite the magnetic field. Notably, the critical point for this phenomenon occurs when the Zeeman energy equals the sum of the spin-orbit and Zeeman splittings, resulting in a chiral breaking of time-reversal symmetry in the superconducting state. Furthermore, increasing the magnetic field beyond this point leads to a modification of the critical temperature, the critical Fascer italicized 's' value, and the spectral function.

By utilizing persistent current mode in a high field NMR system, we collected data in the 14T to 21T range at both 1.6K and 6K. The results show that the vortex lattice exhibits a strong compression along the field line as the magnetic field increases, leading to the H-cutoff phenomenon where the lattice enters a two-dimensional square state along the sample surface at 21T and 1.6K. The vortex lattice's behavior indicates a transition from an Abrikosov state to a sheared or Bose-vortex lattice state at this cutoff point. The vortex lattice's resonance frequency in the high field region provides insight into the pinning force, which appears to increase significantly near the La$_{2.48}$Ba$_{0.47}$H$_{0.01}$ sample's irreversibility line in comparison to other doped Ba-24 samples. The findings also demonstrate the value of high temperature NMR measurements in exploring the deep vortices' behavior within such high magnetic fields.

The well-established "end exclusion" phenomenon, where polymer brush tail chains detach from the surface, has been successfully applied to investigate polymers on curved surfaces. By developing the concept of "end exclusion zones," we refined the mean field theory to reveal that this defect is not inherent but rather a consequence of comparing free energies with a flat reference state. Utilizing the concept of curvature-dependent "pinch points," we created a method to predict where brush defects occur based on the geometry of the surface. Furthermore, a mean field theory was derived that can be used to analyze brush behavior on arbitrary surfaces, successfully modeling configurations like the Earth's surface and a paraboloid. The results indicate that, within the realm of pinch point theory, using a thick brush approximation with the Derjaguin approximation yields comparable outcomes to a precise mean field theory for certain surfaces.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate the quality of images from space, a denoising algorithm called a convolutional neural network was employed on the Fermi 3x3 degree pixel images. Although these images were based on a grid that was 900 times too fine for their purpose, the neural network was successfully tasked with simulating the image quality achievable by the Fermi telescope. Surprisingly, it did so with minimal training data, using around 1000 images. The generated results closely resembled actual all-sky maps produced by the Fermi mission. Moreover, a comparison with mock images generated from an Einstein@Home collaboration showed that the method preserved the brightness and shapes of several well-known sources, like Cas A and 3C 273, while also accurately depicting the diffuse images of some gamma-ray remnants like MWC 0333-33. However, the approach was not entirely flawless, as the sources that appeared multiple times in the data showed some level of artificial repetition in the images. It has also been noted that the method might have potential applications in real data analysis, such as verifying and visually confirming the authenticity of new sources, and removing spurious sources from the existing datasets.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent, upon their turn, makes a choice based on available options from the beginning of their respective turns. We establish a theoretical framework to assess the performance of this approach in problems such as maximum weight independent set, constraint satisfaction, submodular function maximization, and directed Steiner tree. We specifically gauge its efficiency by comparing the quality of solutions produced when modifiable items are selected, in contrast to high-quality solutions achievable when modifiable items are replaced with optima of their respective subsets. We develop analysis techniques and obtain key findings, such as bounding the outcome of combinatorial optimization problems using directed acyclic graph representations, and derive actionable insights into designing effective algorithms for specific problem domains. In particular, we identify scenarios where taking advantage of problem structure allows for leveraging combinatorial optimization algorithms on subsets of instances. As a result, we devise new approximation algorithms for graph-based problems, obtaining improved performance in certain cases.

We have identified 19 unique binary asteroids through a comprehensive analysis of 343,764 Wide Field Camera 3 observations from the Kepler mission. By applying a custom detection algorithm to the data, our study contributes to understanding binary stability and the masses of asteroids. Among the discovered binaries are 14 with exceptionally large separations of over 1000 km. These high mass separations provide valuable insights for theories of binary formation. In collaboration with the NEOWIDE survey, our study also identifies potential weak contacts between some binary components, indicating possible interactions. Additionally, we introduce an efficient method for detecting wide separation binary asteroids using data from the Kepler mission. This approach takes advantage of multiple observations of the same target over an extended period of time to filter out large moving objects and detect the relative motion of binary components. As a result, we are able to detect binary asteroids with a mass separation of over 1.5e19 kg with an 80% confidence level. To improve the sensitivity of this approach, increasing the number of observations and the total duration of the survey both play crucial roles in reducing the mass threshold detectable. With a sufficient number of observations and a total duration of over two years, the sensitivity could be reduced to approximately 1.5e18 kg.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

This paper analyzes the performance of complex MIMO systems that utilize spatial modulation and multiuser detection with a least-squares method, and derives rate and distortion metrics for this setup. By applying an asymptotic characterization, we evaluate specific detector methods, including an optimal Bayesian detector, and develop a simplified approach for optimizing a related detection method, before supporting our findings with numerical simulations.

We've developed an open web platform called SEDfit that enables users to fit
spectral energy distributions (SEDs) to galaxy observations and obtain fitting
parameters from a variety of models.  Users can input their own datasets or
select pre-existing ones from the galaxy catalog on the server.  Once the SED
fitting is complete, users can generate statistical tables and even customized
HTML pages to visually represent the results.  The platform is suitable for
both individual researchers and collaborative projects, such as the DESI
Legacy Survey, and can accommodate large-scale data processing.  With its
modular source code written in Python, Python SQL Alchemy, and JavaScript,
SEDfit is easily extensible to support new galaxy samples, features, and even
custom dashboards.

The South Atlantic rift basin formed during the rifting event that broke up the supercontinent Pangea and gave rise to the South Atlantic Ocean. A detailed Bouguer anomaly map of the basin and its adjacent areas has been compiled utilizing available and newly published gravity data. This compilation has revealed an east-west oriented anomalous Bouguer anomaly feature in the offshore regions of Brazil and West Africa that correlates with the Rio do Rastro lineament which runs through the South African craton. The anomaly feature displays varying widths of up to 200 km across the basin and exhibits the characteristic parabolic shape seen in other rift basins. Seismic models of the lower crust and upper mantle across the basin indicate minimal lithospheric thinning and an abnormal orientation of mantle flow. These findings support the hypothesis that the development of the South African lineament played a crucial role in initiating rift localization and controlling the geological evolution of the South Atlantic.

A proven strategy to enhance multiple tasks using limited labeled data is
unsupervised pre-training.  Despite being a viable approach, contrastive
learning poses challenges in forming relevant pairs for an unsupervised
segmentation task. To circumvent these challenges, our work proposes a
framework combining a unsupervised pre-training technique with a formation
of robust pseudo labels through a multi-task learning framework.  Specifically,
we devise a multi-task learning framework that incorporates task-specific and
shared task-related features. By means of robust pseudo labels formed through
this framework, we perform a contrastive learning. Experiments conducted on the
Cityscapes semantic segmentation benchmark using 1744 training images
(few-shot setting) and 21 classes demonstrate the superiority of our method
over baseline methods.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which will be assessed at the 2023 Dungeons and Dragons World Championship. This event invites the gaming community to compete for the first place in an arena led by a Dungeon Master with specific goals to influence player decisions. Our evaluation of the championship reveals the extraordinary dedication and skill required from a Dungeon Master to achieve these objectives through effective guidance, showcasing their natural persuasion and problem-solving abilities to tackle complex challenges.

Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time. We introduce an iterative framework that leverages both dataset and external knowledge sources to identify new words, standardize them, and refine features within an external word sense space. Our approach achieves 89% F1 score on a benchmark dataset and enables the discovery of 15 emerging word senses, including a newly identified meaning for the term "admin" in the context of online gaming.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes remains an area with significant areas for further investigation. To better understand this connection, researchers are turning to the theory of knots and Foldway analysis for a comprehensive perspective. This study proposes the use of knotoids as a more suitable tool than traditional knot theory, providing the necessary conditions for a membrane-embedded object to fold into itself. Subsequently, various examples of membrane-embedded knotoids are created using simple transformations from existing configurations. By applying a Retraction method to these and other real protein structures, researchers are able to reveal the topological underpinning of these proteins. The findings indicate that topological analysis can offer a more accessible pathway to the understanding of protein chaperones and other proteins influenced by their surroundings.

To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices. Employing a biased parameter transformation, we established a more reliable 2$\sigma$ range for the EDE fraction, determining an optimal value of $\rho_{\rm EDE}^{\rm max}/\rho_{\rm crit}\approx 0.06$.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed exploration of the connections between continuous symmetry breaking within a narrow-gap model and the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone theorem has been conducted. This study delves into various aspects, including the microcausality principle, a non-commutative limit of the model, and the interpretation of model parameters in relation to mass acquisition by fermions and the divergence of the energy-momentum tensor's expectation value. Additionally, it examines the implications of quantum mechanics on the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, utilizing a specific example. The link between the breaking of symmetry and continuous symmetry was also examined in a quantitative manner. A final section compared narrow-gap models with spontaneous symmetry breaking in conventional theory.

Recent studies have highlighted the potential of counterfactual data in enhancing model efficiency and addressing fairness concerns. Nonetheless, the high expense associated with obtaining labeled data for creating such counterfactuals limits their widespread application. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel, low-cost framework called DISCO that leverages generative models to automatically produce large quantities of labeled counterfactual data. By generating diverse treatment conditions through the use of random noise and leveraging their associated labels, DISCO is capable of efficiently creating a substantial dataset for subsequent analysis. Empirical results demonstrate that using this framework to generate counterfactual data allows models to make accurate predictions through ordinary least regression, outperforming the same approach on real-world data. Additionally, DISCO has been successfully applied to a real-world housing scenario, where it generated a large quantity of labeled counterfactual rental records with diverse attributes.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and
neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene has primarily centered on materials displaying strong ionic characteristics. Conversely, we have demonstrated that weaker ionic compounds, namely Cu-based Heusler compounds, can be successfully grown on graphene via remote epitaxy. Utilizing radio frequency magnetron sputtering, we synthesized three distinct Cu-based Heusler compounds - CuGdAlTi, CuMnPtBi, and CuNiSn, examining their structural, electronic, and magnetic properties. Rutherford backscattering spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirmed the presence of graphene beneath these films, indicating the effectiveness of remote epitaxy technique for Heusler compounds. Additionally, we observed room-temperature magnetic and half-metallic behaviors in two of these films through X-ray magnetic diffraction and room-temperature Hall measurements. These outcomes validate remote epitaxy as a production method for high-quality Heusler compounds exhibiting magnetic and half-metallic behaviors. Furthermore, graphene's inherent flexibility and resistance to oxidation may enhance the applicability of these materials in magnetic devices.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from the image of an $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear map. A code is classified as $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive if it can be represented by an $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear map's underlying permutation matrix. This study delves into the characteristics of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes, with a focus on rank, dimension, dimension profile, and distance, and a corresponding analysis of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive codes is also conducted. A key factor in determining the distance of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive codes is identified, and a criterion is established to identify monomial $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive codes. A method is proposed for generating all $\Z_3 \Z_9$-additive codes, and a specific method for determining the distance of these codes is also outlined.

The technology of graded viscosity banks, specifically tapering for polymer flooding,
has been analyzed using various models of mixing zone behavior. By considering different
viscosity functions, researchers have mathematically determined the optimal polymer injection
profile, given transverse flow equilibrium assumptions, for both the Koval and Todd-Longstaff models.
Moreover, a numerical assessment has been conducted to evaluate potential polymer gains relative
to flooding using a finite number of polymer slugs.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in generating conditional data with specific target distributions, resulting in widespread adoption. Unfortunately, many existing implementations lack transparency due to their complex, uninterpretable nature. This study puts GAN filters to the test as a means of creating thermodynamically stable, constrained generations that accurately represent physical phenomena. The theorems derived in this research guarantee that the outputs of these controlled generations remain consistent with the imposed constraints and mathematical models, answering key questions regarding the convergence and differentiability of the model, and offering an efficient solution for training. The proposed method offers a distinct advantage over other approaches by eliminating the need for data perturbation during inference, thereby facilitating direct computation of the generated results. As evidence, we present high-quality, constrained portraits and scenes, along with the capability to manipulate certain physical properties of the data generated, thereby highlighting the model's interpretability and reliability.

This study investigates the property of energy dissipation associated with the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, introducing an upper bound that decreases over time, aligns with the original energy at time zero and as time approaches infinity. The upper bound can be perceived as a nonlocal-in-time modified energy, which includes both the original energy and a term representing the memory effect of the fractional derivative. Several other subfractional models, specifically Adams type, Caputo-Hantorz, and Riemann-Liouville equations, are addressed. Furthermore, we develop finite difference schemes that successfully reduce to the original Allen-Cahn equation when the time fraction beta approaches one. These schemes preserve a discrete version of the modified energy upper bound, leading to an improvement over prior works on the topic.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of the functors defining the state functor's underlying structure, which include elements such as underlying algebra, underlying GNS triple, underlying representation, and underlying morphism. These elements are connected via underlying algebra functors that form a comonadic and monadic framework, and we establish that the resulting functors satisfy Zopch's criterion for exhibiting an adjoint relationship, capturing the intrinsic nature of the algebra's structure.

The origins of gamma-rays in radio galaxies remain unclear, particularly in cases where the gamma-ray signal seems linked to the galaxy's activity level. To explore this connection, we examined the gamma-ray emissions of three types of radio galaxies - those with active supermassive black holes at their centers, blazars, and radio galaxies with less active black holes, or FR I galaxies. By applying a general relationship between a black hole's activity and its gamma-ray emissions, we discovered that the gamma-rays in these less active black holes are best explained by a steady accumulation of matter, with a rate of about 0.02 times the solar mass rate. In contrast, gamma-rays in more active black holes are produced through the conversion of a solar mass rate of matter into energy, or higher. These findings suggest that gamma-ray emissions in these two distinct groups of radio galaxies indeed result from the same underlying process, such as the consumption of matter by the black hole, or the interaction of high-speed particle beams with surrounding gas.

This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods to model portfolio returns, establishing key equations and methodical approaches. By utilizing specific techniques, we can approximate the cumulative distribution function of portfolio returns, based on the individual assets' characteristics. These methods are particularly effective in scenarios where portfolio composition involves either limited high-weighted components or a larger number of evenly weighted components, allowing for more accurate risk measurement and portfolio optimization. We demonstrate our methods through practical examples and visualization techniques, showing significant advantages over conventional models in risk assessment.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and listening to the heart by auscultation is a straightforward yet effective method to listen to heart sounds and identify abnormalities. Listening to the heart is an essential skill taught in medical education and can provide early signs of conditions like murmurs. However, advanced students and professionals often struggle to accurately interpret what they hear, leading to the development of various tools to aid in analyzing heart sounds.

This study introduces a groundbreaking approach to automatically identifying the presence of murmurs by listening to the heart, building on prior work that demonstrated success in classifying normal and abnormal heart sounds. Our method leverages a pre-trained artificial ear to convert sound recordings into spectral features, allowing for more efficient processing of raw audio data. These features are then used to train a machine learning model to detect murmurs. Experimental results indicate that this method achieves a 91.5% accuracy rate in identifying the presence of murmurs by listening to the heart, compared to a 89.0% accuracy rate with traditional feature extraction methods.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices has facilitated seamless health data collection and analysis through wearables. However, significant challenges persist when utilizing these wearables for efficient data aggregation and personalized applications. The primary issues involve securely aggregating data from multiple sources and customizing functionality to individual user needs within a single device. To address these limitations, we present Wearable Personalized Secure Aggregation (W-PASA), a novel approach to securely aggregging data from multiple sources while allowing personalized functionality on wearable devices. The PAPUCA protocol, a cornerstone of W-PASA, enables serverless aggregation of data from wearables without exposing sensitive information to untrusted parties. Additionally, we demonstrate how an extended version of PAPUCA supports wearable personalization, allowing users to customize functionality while preserving data privacy. Our evaluation of 10,000 simulated wearable instances highlights the efficiency and practicality of W-PASA.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

A comprehensive theory of string compactifications, known as Control-KKLTT, is proposed with the aim of unifying dark and baryogenesis phenomena in the early universe. The study involves analyzing vacuum solutions, calculating effective action, and exploring the possibility of de Sitter vacuums through bubble nucleation. The results demonstrate that dark energy arises naturally from solutions related to the F-term and the universe's ultimate destiny remains uncertain due to the potential for AdS decay. Additionally, the study shows that satisfying conditions for electroweak symmetry breaking also allows for successful baryon number production, utilizing both thermal and non-thermal mechanisms within bubble walls.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a well-known computational issue. While individual research has been conducted on these issues, an unconnected body of knowledge emerges. We address this by proposing an integrated framework for crafting interview schedules in substantial organizations. Our comprehensive model accounts for elements such as multiple interview panels, a balance between groupings and randomizations in testing, and varied durations associated with each applicant. Due to the inherent complexity of our formulation, an innovative variant of genetic algorithms is developed to produce highly effective interview schedules within reasonable timeframes. We tested this approach through rigorous experimentation and compared its outcomes with real-world industry practices. Our data indicates that our method yields significantly more optimal results than traditional methods. To demonstrate the advantages of our technique, a user-friendly web interface has been released at the following URL: https://interview.ycsa.cs.sjtu.edu.cn/.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the underlying process. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying process cannot transition to certain states, showing how this limitation influences the optimality conditions.

To explore the significance of new physics, our research focuses on asymmetric leptoquark pair creation within the context of proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, with energies of 13 and 125 TeV. As leptoquarks carry both baryon and lepton charges, their formation results in prominent jet activity, potentially offering a means to differentiate them from background noise. To achieve this, we apply jet selection criteria to signal and background distributions, with jet kinematics adjusted to match those of widely observed jet anomalies. To accommodate a broad spectrum of leptoquark masses, from 500 GeV to 10 TeV, we calculate leptoquark formation rates, considered in both color-singlet and color-octet forms, and determine corresponding limits on leptoquark mass, leveraging data sets of 35 and 90 inverse femtobarns. To facilitate future research, we provide leptoquark decay product distributions, as well as formation rates, spanning the entire mass range. Temporal sequence analysis typically involves applying supervised learning methods, but many existing techniques struggle to capture both classification and temporal dependencies. Existing approaches often fail to effectively model global temporal patterns due to their limited, local learning rules. Our novel method, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time (SGTM-TT), addresses this issue by creating a global low-dimensional representation that preserves temporal structure. By incorporating an entropy-based cost function and a corresponding learning rule, SGTM-TT simultaneously minimizes the difference between input and projected data while preserving both topological and temporal characteristics. Our algorithmic modification enables the resolution of complex temporal patterns in our experimental evaluations on synthetic time series, medical imaging, and speech recognition, demonstrating the method's effectiveness in accurate temporal pattern recognition.

Most estimates of gas temperature based on carbon emissions are unreliable as they rely on a process that was incomplete, which can skew line profiles and result in line widths that are too narrow, potentially affecting line widths that are related to line profiles. As a consequence, the observed line broadening is a combination of lines that are affected by incomplete excitation and lines that are not representative of the overall gas motion. In addition, the observed line broadening is a combination of lines that are affected by different lines of sight. We tackle current, striking discrepancies in flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson systems, addressing issues with CP-violating Kaon decay and lepton flavor violation, while resolving longstanding problems with the direct CKM matrix element $|V_{us}|$ and the CKM unitarity triangle's angle $\epsilon_K$. The proposed solution involves introducing heavy flavor gauge bosons associated with new $U_{\rm PQCSD}$ flavor symmetries, specifically through the introduction of heavy quark currents that transform under new flavor symmetries in a way that ensures the cancellation of anomalies with the standard model sector, under the assumption of new flavor symmetries being self-anomalous. The proposed gauge groups $U_{\rm PQCSD} = U_Q \otimes U_{\rm PSD}$ consist of product groups formed by flavor symmetry factors $U_Q$ and $\{\rm 1,~5,~7,~11,~13,~17,~19,~23,~29,~31\}$, where the letter $Q$ denotes quarks, while the other letters denote leptons, color septets, and pseudo-singlets, respectively. The introduced model is tested through flavor-changing neutral currents, particularly through the introduction of heavy lepton states, which serve as the primary decay products of the proposed flavor gauge bosons.

Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 1985 with a varied version of the traditional approach. In the classic version of this approach, an infinite number of parallel wires are used. In this setup, an infinite sequence of symbols from a given alphabet is transmitted. At each wire, a noisy version of a finite segment of the original sequence is received by the decoder. The decoder then attempts to reconstruct the original infinite sequence based on all the received noisy segments. In this report, we adopt a more direct approach to this approach. Specifically, we determine the minimum number of wires required to recover the original infinite sequence, according to the majority voting principle.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but the current generation of Question Answering systems struggle to grasp the complex relationships between different information within the paper and to interpret the nuanced language used, resulting in subpar performance. The development of these systems is further hindered by the lack of large datasets that pair question references with the specific parts of the documents they relate to. To address this challenge, we introduce QReLiC, a novel question answering dataset that comprises approximately 10k human-written pairs of questions and their related segments from long-form sources, such as research papers, technical reports, and videos, thereby providing a valuable resource for the task of question answering across various domains and facilitating the further study of this challenging task.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction in processing time by over four orders of magnitude compared to numerical approaches based on post-Newtonian expansions. The findings also reveal that analytic expressions retain an acceptable level of accuracy when the angle of the orbit is moderate to extreme, even close to the point of coalescence, and that these expressions retain validity up to radii of 10 times the gravitational length scale. Furthermore, we propose that these findings lay the groundwork for enhancing the range and proximity of these expressions in order to maintain robustness close to the 3/2 post-Newtonian order.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a position balanced relative to time as time grows indefinitely, as evidenced by a rescaled displacement $X(t)/t$ that equals a specific constant for all sufficiently large values of $t$, as demonstrated after $t$ exceeds an exponential times power of $t$, with probability approaching one.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods. A unified framework is established, highlighting areas that require further investigation, including model development, statistical analysis, and educational research.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential.

Acronyms serve as a crucial means of abbreviation in modern language and are present in nearly all languages. While acronyms are widely used in texts, their interpretation can sometimes be difficult, particularly when the referred entities are not well-known. To address this issue, acronym resolution has emerged as an essential acronym-related task. Many previous studies focused on acronym resolution utilized datasets in the English language. However, there are relatively few English resources available, and no studies to date have explored this task in the Polish language. The objective of our work was to adapt the existing English dataset for Polish and, as a result, we collected and annotated a corpus comprising 700 entries from Polish Wikipedia articles. The annotation included determining whether the acronym's target was a named entity, a common noun, or unknown. To test our hypotheses, we employed the proposed dataset and utilized the linear models, as well as the transformer-based models. The results from the experiment were presented to validate our findings.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between spin-exchange collisions, photoassociation with two opposing frequencies, and two-photon bound-state formation results in robust dimer creation. Since spin-exchange collisions cannot alter total angular momentum, they primarily facilitate atom-atom conversion within the same spin sector. To address interactions with continuum states, we employed an effective model accounting for both discrete and continuous spectra. We experimentally demonstrated our approach using a disk-shaped loss diagram, derived from the Redfield equation, to monitor both atomic and molecular populations. By addressing various scenarios with distinct initial conditions and interaction strengths, we showed that the model is feasible with current technology and may be feasible with present technology. We anticipate that this method could also be useful for studying the dynamics of molecular formation in other unison phases.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects through object pointers, rather than a flat collection of objects. Objects, composed of stacked DNA tiles, store data in a compact form. The architecture enables a flexible data update process by targeting specific objects, and supports both granular and cost-effective modifications. Moreover, the system facilitates straightforward data retrieval via object parsing, and the organization of objects aligns with the hierarchical data access pattern, facilitating efficient searching. To validate the architecture, we developed the QMARS parser and demonstrated its performance with large datasets, showing superior data access speeds and manageable storage costs due to the alignment of DNA objects with the data hierarchy.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research due to their exceptional quantum property of robust, dissipation-free electron flow. These properties are linked to topological characteristics, which can be thought of as the winding behavior of a system's underlying structure in a mathematical space. In this paper, we develop a general theoretical framework to analyze topological characteristics through the lens of random matrix theory, focusing on both simple and complex matrix ensembles. By applying this framework, we derive specific matrix representations for topological phases, such as Chern insulators and TI thin films. Our approach unifies existing matrix-based descriptions and provides a systematic method to study properties like conductance and energy gaps in these systems.

A brain tumor affects the central nervous system and is the most prevalent neurological malignancy globally.  When it comes to brain tumor detection and diagnosis, MRI is the primary imaging technique used.  MRI technology provides detailed images of soft tissues, making it an effective method for tumors.  Neural networks have revolutionized medical image processing, leading to significant advancements in brain tumor detection and segmentation using MRI scans.  In this study, we evaluated several state-of-the-art algorithms for detection and segmentation of brain tumors using MRI scans.  Specifically, we tested nine different detection models and three segmentation algorithms.  We assessed these models' performance based on brain tumor–positive rates, accuracy, and Dice scores.  Our research indicates that the UNet algorithm achieved the best segmentation results, while the ResNet50 model exhibited superior detection accuracy.  All models developed in this research are publicly available on the GitHub platform.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their inability to handle complex physical phenomena or by their inability to efficiently process large-scale and high-resolution scenes. This research presents an advanced differentiable renderer that effectively addresses both challenges, capable of simulating intricate physical processes such as subsurface scattering and participating media scattering while also delivering remarkable real-time performance of 100 frames per second across four high-resolution scenes with complex light transport. The developer achieves this by utilizing a meticulously crafted light cache-based radiosity algorithm that provides an unbiased solution, in conjunction with forward multi-bounce Monte Carlo path tracing to precisely compute the scattering processes and surface scattering processes.

A popular technique, widely used in video technology over the last half-century, is interlacing. This technique reduces transmission bandwidth by half, combining two slightly offset images from consecutive half-frames. Presently, high-definition broadcasts rely on scanning all the lines in video frames, yet the human eye perceives more detail in vertical than horizontal directions. To enhance image quality, a super-resolution method has been developed to restore lost high-frequency details in video, utilizing interlacing. These methods transform both half-frames into progressive frames, then apply conventional super-resolution techniques. Nonetheless, this approach either doubles the computation for converting interleaved to progressive frames or results in enhanced half-frames of differing sizes. In response, we propose a novel concurrent deinterlacing and super-resolution method that transforms both half-frames to enhanced progressive frames of equal size simultaneously. Our technique leverages bidirectional data flow between the deinterlacing and SR processes, constructing an optimization model that considers both SR and deinterlacing objectives. By minimizing the total objective function using an alternative algorithm, we achieve an improved outcome. Comparative testing shows our method surpasses existing deinterlacing and SR methods, particularly in areas rich with detail.

The investigation revealed a disparity of approximately 0.1 fm in the root mean square radius of the neutron point distribution between non-relativistic mean field models and their relativistic counterparts. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to varying product values of the effective mass and one-body potential strength within the respective frameworks, with those values being governed by the Hugenholtz-Van Hove theorem. In contrast, the thickness of the neutron skin was found not to solely correlate with the symmetry potential but rather was heavily dependent on the nucleon effective mass.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as enhancing flow measurement, improving flood forecasting, and facilitating real-time flow control. While the traditional method employs numerical solvers to calculate velocities from flow images, this approach can be computationally expensive and slow for real-world scenarios. To address this challenge, a linear regression model was developed to solve the two-dimensional horizontal projection of the two-dimensional scalar potential equation, which describes the two-dimensional velocity field. This novel method leverages machine learning algorithms to calculate river flow velocities from images. To train the model, a random forest model was utilized, and its performance was evaluated on a public dataset of three Brazilian rivers. The results showed that the machine learning model outperformed the traditional finite difference method in both accuracy and speed, achieving a mean absolute error of 0.19 velocity meters per second. The proposed method offers a practical and efficient alternative to traditional numerical solvers for velocity field calculations from images.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone
images by utilizing the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative
image fusion method is introduced, leveraging optimization and weighted averages.
These techniques are applied to a mobile HDR application, demonstrating the
feasibility of the approach. Comparative assessments are also conducted to
demonstrate the introduced solution's efficiency and effectiveness in comparison to
established methods.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within machine learning and causal inference. In response to these challenges, the Causal Deep Learning Challenge was created with the goal of establishing a benchmark for methods in this field. This paper provides a detailed account of the challenge, including an outline of the process, the development of the BIANCA dataset, and the various stages of the challenge. Additionally, the paper reports the results and findings from the 2021 and 2022 competitions, including a discussion of the winning algorithms, the overall performance, and the associated lessons learned.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings in these systems is often hindered by limited access to intrusive sensors. This research proposes a method for estimating temperature profiles in reactive gas systems using non-invasive optical sensors, specifically OES, in combination with machine learning algorithms. Initially, a dataset was created to train the machine learning model, which could predict the temperature profiles of the entire reactor. Subsequently, a novel approach was developed to generate datasets for further testing and validation of the machine learning model. The results demonstrated the effectiveness of using OES and machine learning in obtaining accurate temperature readings within catalytic fixed bed reactors, without the need for intrusive sensors.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, for which the Equivalent B-principle is proven, and is shown to follow from the principles of directed submersions. Additionally, our research demonstrates that any map within the category of directed colored broken submersions can be replaced by a map within the principle of submersions, and that the principle of directed colored broken submersions is equivalent to the principle of maps between the spaces involved.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is conducted here, focusing on right-preconditioning with both classical and high-order finite element discretizations. Key aspects examined include the impact of using different finite element grids on the accuracy of the solution, as well as an in-depth analysis of how the problem's condition number is affected by these grids through the examination of the problem's eigenvalues.

The standard scaled Wigner matrix is a symmetric $n\times n$ matrix $W_n$ with independent Gaussian entries $W_{ij}^2$ following chi-square distributions. As $n$ increases, these matrices converge in law to an infinite-dimensional operator known as the semi-circular element $s$, which is derived from a free Gaussian element with unit variance. The second power of $n$ times the trace of the $n$-th matrix power $w_n^k$ is determined by summing the products of matrix entry values for each sequence of indices, which is equivalent to summing over non-crossing pair-partitions of the set $\{1,\ldots,k\}$. Non-crossing pair-partitions are in one-to-one correspondence with the number of ways to partition a triangle into quadrilaterals along the edges of that triangle, or alternatively as the sum of areas of regions defined by hyperbolic inequalities. This alternative representation allows us to establish an upper bound on the number of non-crossing pair-partitions.

Persuasive promotional videos, created with a specific objective in mind, are highly effective and widely employed in various settings. Recent advancements in video technology have enabled non-professionals to make them, yet navigating the complex design process remains a daunting task. To address this challenge, our research focuses on developing a comprehensive framework that leverages artificial intelligence to create compelling promotional videos. Our approach involves three essential steps: using text-based tools to design video content and style based on user input, developing multiple video options through image-based editing, and refining the final product through text-based feedback. The application of our system in real-world scenarios has demonstrated its ability to produce more compelling and cohesive promotional videos that align closely with user requirements and provide a satisfactory user experience.

Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily circumvented through trivial methods like cutting the attack path. Our research challenges the assumption that most contemporary defenses rely on flawed techniques and successfully create robust defenses without employing gradient masking. Utilizing the adversarial example generated by a basic attack, we conducted an exhaustive evaluation of 11 widely cited defense methods across three distinct datasets. Notably, our study is the first to thoroughly examine the transferability of adversarial examples against these defenses at a small perturbation level, typically seen in practical scenarios. The primary discoveries from our research are as follows: initially, many of the surveyed defense methods demonstrate remarkable resilience to adversarial examples with low transferability; subsequently, we pinpointed the gradient masking mechanism as the cause in select cases, confirming the efficacy of gradient masking attack as the primary explanation; and, intriguingly, we observed the phenomenon of over-defense, in which the combination of two attack path-circumventing layers is more easily bypassed than a single vulnerable defense. The outcome of our comprehensive evaluation indicates that the majority of the surveyed defense methods do not rely on the gradient masking mechanism and can withstand adversarial examples even with minimal transferability.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, including flat acoustic lenses and sound cloaks. However, designing and fabricating these metagratings according to specifications is a complex process. Our research introduces an efficient iterative integral equation method tailored for high-contrast periodic structures, accurately predicting their acoustic scattering properties while accounting for multiple scatterings and implicit periodic boundary conditions. By applying this method to verify numerical microlens models, we demonstrated its capability to accurately predict the Bianisotropic microlens models' performance in focusing scattered waves at specific distances, lens diameters, and frequencies. Furthermore, the method's computational speed and accuracy make up to 95-100% accurate in forecasting the microlens models' performance.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time, a finding that may have implications for tracking organisms in their habitats using methods such as radio collars and genetic analysis.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators. This framework allows for a consistent treatment of modes with distinct frequencies, taking into account modes that are both weakly and strongly coupled. The approach leads to the creation of generalized equations of motion for the modes' amplitudes. These equations can accurately model a wide range of phenomena, including solitons, bistability, multistability, mode splitting, red-shifting, and mode merging. As an illustration, the theory is applied to a Fabry-Perot optical resonator.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in control systems that allow unbounded controls, encompassing polynomial control systems. Our analysis specifically addresses unbounded open-loop controls and discontinuous feedback stabilizers, which may lead to trajectories exhibiting chattering behavior near the target. A central aspect of our findings is the demonstration of the equivalence between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in the described context, effectively resolving an open question from a previous study.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flows with longitudinal forcing. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical distributions based on four low-resolution input data. Furthermore, it exhibited better energy spectrum representation compared to conventional regression models trained with the same dataset.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration. It addresses and resolves issues with previously published versions of the equations by deriving a correct formulation. The paper also explores various applications, including an explicit solution related to charge oscillation, connecting to classic resonance phenomena. Additionally, the equations' quantum aspect is discussed, along with their connection to radiation fields and quantum Rabi oscillations.

The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers, however, frequently suffer from poor calibration. This issue poses a significant problem, given the increasing use of these systems in critical applications. Our research proposes a novel method to enhance the calculation of probabilistic outputs for deep neural network classifiers. This improved method, an uncertainty-aware margin softmax (UAMS) loss function, delivers superior results in terms of calculating accurate probability estimates. Notably, the UAMS loss function's performance surpasses that of other prominent methods, including adaptive softmax (AS) and label smoothing (LS). Moreover, the benefits of UAMS can be applied across various neural network architectures. Furthermore, by introducing the concept of uncertainty calibration, we demonstrate the value of the UAMS method in prioritizing more reliable data points for optimal model fine-tuning.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic, ever-changing environments. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to recover from unforeseen situations they have not encountered during training. Many real-world settings, including image recognition and navigation, involve complex and intricate tasks that require robust solutions capable of adapting to novel situations. This paper introduces the concept of latent action encoding, a novel framework that addresses these challenges by generating high-dimensional, semantically meaningful action representations through unsupervised learning. This approach enables simple neural network policies to utilize these encoded actions for effective unsupervised feature learning and task execution, thereby facilitating the acquisition of new tasks without explicit supervision and promoting generalization in dynamic, unstructured environments.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, which analyze data traces to reveal the underlying structure of processes. Despite this capability, a significant challenge persists in addressing gaps within process models that fail to accurately reflect real-world scenarios. These models inoperable in practical scenarios, such as predicting the outcomes of intentional changes made by process participants or automated systems aimed at optimizing specific objectives. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel approach that treats process models as potentially incomplete representations and aims to learn their potential goals to predict behavioral changes resulting from subsequent real-world interventions. Our method is based on a family of goal-based process models comprising activity priorities and application of process discovery techniques in reverse, which A) unifies and extends existing work on process goal learning, and for the first time, employs process goal learning to identify process model incompleteness and address it by filling the gaps with the most probable missing goal-based process model elements.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for some states, representing an unusual phenomenon. Additionally, this occurrence can be understood through a mathematical model that represents dimerized interactions over extended distances.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck Adaptive Optics system to enhance its capabilities. Now under construction, Liger will be available starting in 2020 and optimized for observing wavelengths between 0.95 and 2.5 micrometers. The 1050-telescope features 15 guidance channels and can gather up to 15 million pixels per second, making it suitable for a variety of observing methods including spectroscopy, imaging, and spectrophotometry. Liger will be capable of simultaneously observing up to 30 spectra with as little as 3000 resolution, or a 15-times greater number of spectra at higher resolution. The Liger instrument team has established a comprehensive set of 35 primary scientific goals that span the study of solar system objects, stellar systems, stellar dynamics, star and black hole activity, stellar remnants, nebulae, galaxy evolution, and the study of distant stars and systems beyond our own.

Optical systems using amplitude masks face a severe resolution restriction known as Rayleigh's curse, which directly correlates with the system's aperture ratio. Researchers have managed to bypass this limitation in various ways, albeit with significant light intensity sacrifices. In an effort to overcome this constraint, we investigate a coherent detection optical system where the input point source is positioned in close proximity to the system's input plane, effectively removing the ratio that limits resolution. By developing an analytical analytical resolution limit formula for this system, we discovered that the resolution could be decoupled from the aperture ratio. Furthermore, the system retains flexibility in optimizing the mask without being constrained to pass only the central system component. Through both theoretical and practical experiments, we demonstrated the system's capability to resolve distinct points of light, along with the ability to maintain pattern fidelity and optimize contrast through mask design.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning signs of sudden population shifts is of great importance. A recent study found that a biological system with two interacting species, experiencing chaotic, irregular fluctuations known as mixed-mode oscillations, may exhibit warning signs of stable behavior. Based on this finding, the researchers developed a model, and then used a numerical approach to analyze the conditions under which the mixed-mode and stable states coexist. A new criterion was also established to predict the occurrence of mixed-mode oscillations, and further demonstrated with a specific ecosystem model consisting of plant, herbivore, and predator species.

Determining whether bulge growth is primarily through mergers or internal processes remains a key question in understanding the formation of galaxies. This study aims to provide evidence of rapid star formation in the inner regions of galaxies that cannot be attributed to mergers. By analyzing the relationship between the growth rate of galaxies and their structural properties, we found a distinct pattern in the data that is consistent with a specific ratio of formation rates in bulges and galaxies as a whole, particularly in early-type galaxies. This evidence is derived from an examination of the non-linear connection between a galaxy's formation rate and its structural properties, including the star formation rate threshold in galaxies that exhibits the steepest change in behavior. This critical threshold corresponds to a specific difference in logarithmic scale between the formation rates of bulges and galaxies that is around -1.8, which is in line with the theoretical ratio derived from galaxy merger simulations (-1.76). This ratio is unrelated to the properties of disks in galaxies, thus allowing us to identify the internal star formation rate in bulges that is around 20 times lower than the total star formation rate in gas-rich galaxies with a index of around 2.8. This distinct pattern in the data is evidence of a fundamental difference in the formation mechanisms of bulges and galaxies, thus providing a crucial guideline in the search for an underlying physical process that drives this specific difference.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the emotional tone in YouTube video descriptions related to COVID-20 vaccines. Initially, a traditional method using labeled data is outlined. Then, two innovative approaches are detailed: one leveraging a descriptive video description dataset expanded through back-translation of labeled data, and another utilizing a clustering technique on unlabeled data from multiple languages. Ultimately, the cluster centroids are manually classified.

Recent proposals for cache coherence protocols, such as self-invalidation and self-downgrade, have shown promising results in reducing overhead and enhancing scalability, particularly for large systems with multiple shared caches. However, these systems' reliance on hierarchical cache structures has limited their applicability in emerging flat memory systems that forgo such hierarchy. This research introduces the first coherence protocol, called SEEP, operating on a flat shared-cache system based on self-invalidating and self-downgrading principles. By combining invalidation and data marking in the caches, SEEP ensures correct data access while minimizing invalidation messages, thus overcoming limitations of prior protocols. Experimental results indicate that SEEP outperforms existing systems on such platforms, showing particularly advantageous outcomes for systems with three or more shared caches.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions.

Let $f : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^d$ be a function defined on the unit interval. The fractional Hausdorff and Minkowski dimensions of the set $E = f([0,1])$ are crucial in determining the properties of the occupation measure $\mu(s,t) = \int_0^s \delta_B(f(r), t) \, \mathrm{d}r$ for $0 \le s \le 1$, Borel sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and Dirac measures. If the function $f$ is Lipschitz continuous, the question arises as to the conditions under which $\mu$ belongs to the $L^2$ space. This is related to whether the parabolic Hausdorff dimension of the graph of $f$ meets a specific requirement, namely if its dimension is at least the integer part of $d/2$ plus $d/2$. This condition has applications in various fields, including multiple fractional integration by parts formulas, stochastic Fock space theory, and multiple Wiener–Itô integrals.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield results indicating that quantum fluctuations can provoke chaotic behavior in regions of the H\'enon-Heiles system that classically remain stable.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics, or semantic features, which have been shown to correlate with patient disease progression.  These features may offer valuable information that can aid in forecasting the likelihood of severe COVID-19 symptoms. Nonetheless, it's unclear to what degree radiologists consciously utilize this information when forming their predictions.  To shed light on this issue, we applied advanced techniques to visualize the regions of the images that AI models focus on when making their assessments. Our findings suggest that the AI models are centrating on areas consistent with pulmonary symptoms, thereby providing an encouraging validation of the method's accuracy.  To further confirm the practical value of image-based features in predicting severe cases, we analyzed the predictions made by the AI models for several actual clinical cases.  Our results reveal that hand-crafted image features combined with historical patient data can effectively predict severe outcomes, achieving a satisfactory accuracy rate.  This study has the potential to inform the development of more effective clinical support tools.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD).
