A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation and regularization methods to enhance unsupervised medical image segmentation. The proposed method initially generates an initial segmentation through clustering, followed by optimization using a combination of boundary and shape regularization terms. Specifically, the method takes the dictionary learned from contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI images and applies it to non-contrast MRI images to improve segmentation accuracy. The proposed approach achieves superior results compared to other methods in terms of overall segmentation accuracy, as demonstrated by experimental results on public T1-weighted MRI images.

To fully utilize the upgraded Large Hadron Collider, a comprehensive upgrade to the jet detection system is necessary. The new system will involve upgrading and expanding the existing JETCAT processor framework to create JECMAP. This will include a significant increase in input data handled by the system, along with modifications to the software framework that will allow for a fully integrated approach to jet calibration within individual experiments. This framework will be compatible with both simple and sophisticated pattern recognition techniques used for jet calibration.

By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering would greatly enhance its
versatility, but current research has primarily focused on static objects and excludes
dynamic human models. We investigate the possibility of rendering dynamic humans using
an articulated neural approach, and in doing so, we explore the potential of such a
method to efficiently re-use a foundational model across multiple scenarios, thereby
overcoming limitations associated with traditional rendering techniques. We
demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, named Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR), in
creating high-quality virtual human avatars that are articulated and realistic, and
which can be personalized with a single image. ANR's modularity allows for easy
extension to include non-rigid body models.

To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's essential to accurately assess local atomic disorder within them. This study 
introduced a novel approach to measuring the disorder parameter based on the peak 
width in a differential pair of peaks in a diffraction pattern. The method was 
applied to analyze the disorder in the oxide layer of a laser metal deposition 
sample made of 316L stainless steel. The measure of the disorder parameter obtained 
from the diffraction data correlates with the results from the micro-hardness 
measurements. The proposed disorder parameter can be determined non-destructively 
and at a distance, offering a means to monitor material performance and 
interactively guide the heat treatment process to adjust the microstructure and 
enhance the mechanical properties of the material.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\kappa(\theta)$ from this family is equivalent to $\kappa(\theta^*)$ where $\theta^*$ is from $\Omega$ if there exists a mapping $h$ from $\theta$ to $\theta^*$ such that $f(y|\theta) = f(y|\theta^*)$ for all $\theta, \theta^* \in \Omega$ implies $\theta = h^{-1}(\theta^*)$. This work addresses estimating a mixed distribution $E_\theta f(y|\theta)$ from an unknown $\theta$ based on independent and identically distributed data, given that the set of $\theta$ is the range of $h$ and $f$ is monotonically decreasing. Under the condition that $\theta$ is not log-concave but $\theta h(\theta)$ is, we have developed consistent Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however most of these approaches rely heavily on hyperparameter tuning, resulting in increased computational costs and complexity in real-world deployment. This research introduces a novel knowledge tracing framework that necessitates minimal hyperparameter adjustment. By integrating a simple yet effective component, our model automatically identifies and corrects regions of overfitting in complex deep learning models, thereby enhancing students' performance predictions. The proposed method achieves superior results across multiple established benchmarks, outperforming leading deep learning-based knowledge tracing models. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, extensive experiments were conducted, illustrating the capacity of our method to generalize across diverse datasets and minimize hyperparameter sensitivity. The source code is openly accessible on GitHub (https://github.com/zhengqian99/EF-KT).

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's proof format debuted,  
which has undergone significant evolution ever since. veriT's proofs have found a  
wide range of applications and numerous solvers now generate proofs in this same  
format. As the next step in further improvement, we would like to hear feedback  
from the community to guide upcoming developments in this area. This feedback will  
be utilized in looking at the format's past progression, presenting the approach  
that guided its development, as well as the problems other solvers may experience  
in utilizing it.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on this concept, our research extends FedBuff to the xDSL network, a widely used narrowband communication system tailored for low-latency, secure transmission in limited bandwidth environments. The FedBuff algorithm was adapted to fit the constraints of the xDSL system, specifically addressing its unique security requirements and limited communication capabilities. Our findings showcase the benefits of FedBuff in enhancing throughput when dealing with larger client groups, with the potential to accelerate the convergence of cross-device federated learning.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without changing sound-letter mappings and were able to obtain very accurate Czech ASR even with only one extra day's worth of training data after using the English model. This concept was further demonstrated with Czech model's adaptation for Slovak, achieving nearly perfect Czech-to-Slovak ASR transfer. We open the idea of intermediate alphabet for transfer learning across language barriers particularly for resource-constrained languages.

Graph mining applications rely heavily on node embeddings that preserve structure and proximity. To test the validity of novel node embedding techniques, a limited range of benchmark datasets is typically used. In this study, a new diverse social network dataset, Twitch Gamers, has been created to provide a range of target attributes. The evaluation of the social network and the results of the node classification experiments confirm that Twitch Gamers is suitable for assessing the effectiveness of novel node embedding algorithms.

Our study proposes that a previous observation made by the LHCb collaboration, 
which was based on the $f_0(980)$ and $f_0(1370)$ di-kaon decay channels, 
of a state near $T_{\text{CC}}$ compositeness threshold, is actually the $\epsilon$ 
resonance. To support this claim, we present results from Monte Carlo analyses 
of experimental data by the LHCb and the Belle collaborations. These analyses 
demonstrate that the LHCb and Belle observations, of a state at a mass of 420 MeV 
with a width of 60-100 MeV, are consistent with scaled signals of a narrow 
resonance known as the $\epsilon$ with an production rate of approximately 
$10^{-2}$ times that of the $f_0(980)$ in $J/\psi$ decays, or a significant 
excess of the $\epsilon$ relative to the $\epsilon$ in $B$-meson decays. 
Additionally, we suggest that the $\epsilon$ could be identified as a molecular 
configuration of two $K\bar{K}$ components. A deeper investigation into the 
apparent width anomaly of the $\epsilon$ is also presented in this study.

Recent research suggests that the dark sector could resolve the ultraviolet divergence problem associated with the cosmic background and the missing mass issue. Building upon this, our study investigates the dark dimension's potential influence on the evaporation process of black holes and the release of heavy particles trapped within them. Using a model based on an extra dimension with specific dark matter properties similar to the cosmic background, we found the rate of Hawking radiation increases significantly, particularly for smaller black holes. However, for larger black holes, the radiation rate is constrained by the cosmic background and they remain in a stable equilibrium. In this equilibrium state, black holes effectively act as natural dark matter particles. We discovered the model predicts a specific equilibrium mass that could potentially be identified through experiments, such as those conducted with the LHC.

A novel algorithm for precise force control in series elastic actuators is introduced in this paper, centered on a cutting-edge force estimation technique called the transmission force observer. This approach was developed to enhance the inaccurate force readings caused by the nonlinear elastic transmission and sensor measurement errors of the actuators' deformation sensors. The study first critiques conventional SEA force sensing methods, examining their stochastic properties that ultimately enable accurate force control through the proposed transmission force observer. A critical parameter derived from system analysis is key in optimizing the performance of the force-controlled system, guiding the achievement of the system's steady-state accuracy, which is proven feasible under certain conditions, and illustrated with simulation and experimental results.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately dictates the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments.

We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate degenerate, multi-component complex scalar fields. These scalar fields are part of the fundamental representation of both the SU(Nc) gauge group and the global U(Nf) symmetry group. We've investigated how different quartic potential scalar options, in combination with varying mass values, influence the pattern of global symmetry breaking and the mass of the dilaton. Our research has utilized the Monte Carlo method to explore the impact of the quartic potential on global symmetry breaking patterns, demonstrating that in the regime where the scalar potential's quartic term (u) is much less than the product of the scalar field's lambda and g (g^4), a pattern of spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs where (Nf+Nc) and U(Nf)xSU(Nc) symmetries are violated. We've also found evidence indicating that in a regime where u is much less than g^4, a pattern of spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs where (Nf+Nc) and U(Nf)xSU(Nc) symmetries are broken. Additionally, we've explored how the mass of the dilaton changes in response to variations in the scalar potential's quartic term (u) in a regime where u is much, much less than g^4, demonstrating that a pattern of spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs where (Nf+Nc) and U(Nf)xSU(Nc) symmetries are broken.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by reducing TD learning sample requirements.  By leveraging the uncertainty inherent in Gaussian Process predictions, we develop an effective GPGS policy that prevents excessive exploration.  To validate our technique, we compare it to standard TD learning methods using a underwater vehicle navigation task.  Our results show an improvement in navigation success rates of over 90% on a marine simulator.  We achieve this result by demonstrating that our method is highly effective at guiding Unmanned Underwater Vehicles through the complexities of their underwater environment.

This paper explores the concept of sorting networks, specifically those with a fixed number of comparison layers (constant-depth sorting networks). We analyzed the relationship between the number of input elements and the comparators' fixed comparison limits in these networks. Our research found that, within a fixed number of comparison layers, sorting networks with comparatively less input elements allow for comparators with a greater comparison range. In contrast, networks with greater input elements necessitate comparators with a more restricted comparison range. We also developed the rate of change model to describe this relationship and found that our model aligns with existing data across a wide range of input sizes (from 4! to 100!).

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star composed of an anisotropic fluid in two spacetime curvatures, encompassing both type A and type D type/DWEC components. By directly solving the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in a type A DWEC scenario for the type A fluid, and subsequently using the appropriate field equations for type D DWEC, we derive the same metric function $B(r)$ but different volume element function $\Theta(r)$ for the two scenarios. This study examines various physical and causality conditions, and results show that both fluids adhere to these constraints, with type D DWEC fluid also meeting the first and second Hadronic theorems and satisfying the gravitational and strong clustering conditions.

Using recent observations, we create a set of models for a galaxy like the Milky Way. By combining collisionless and gaseous particle simulations, we observe a bar that forms within 1 billion years and influences the galaxy's structure, creating spiral arms, a bulge, and a disk. These simulations reveal the bar's gravitational effect on a galaxy's structure, accelerating star formation in its ends, which contributes to the formation of bulge and thick disk components. However, the bar's presence hinders disk growth, resulting in a disk with low rotation speed and high vertical thickness. Additionally, we note the importance of star formation in the inner regions of the galaxy in determining its overall structure, particularly its central supermassive black hole.

Galactic mergers significantly influence galaxy evolution, especially those involving massive galaxies. While the effects of smaller mergers are well understood, the impact of major mergers on galaxy morphology remains unclear. Using the high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations from the LEGRAM project, we investigated how the morphology of massive gas-rich galaxies is affected by a single equal-mass merger. Our results show a clear dependence of morphological features on the merger outcome, with distinct differences observed between galaxies that merge to form an elliptical galaxy and those that retain a disk. Additionally, our results reveal a strong correlation between the post-merger morphology and the properties of an underlying stellar bulge, providing valuable insights into galaxy formation processes.

Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network. This innovative approach involved initially training two segmentation networks to identify lung regions and inner lesions. Next, we extracted relevant features using the Contrastive Knowledge Distillation module. Lastly, the Contrastive Mixup Classification network performed the severity classification. Our approach was mathematically optimized to minimize classification errors, and we carefully fine-tuned the model to produce accurate results. To validate our solution, we submitted 20 validation tests and achieved a remarkable macro F1-score of 0.793, significantly outperforming the baseline of 0.600.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more accurate pseudo data at a single level. They often overlook the issue of creating high-quality Pseudo Parallel (PSP) datasets from single-pass sequences. Furthermore, the models are typically trained to address errors in isolation, disregarding the need to train them across diverse domains. To tackle these limitations, we initially enhance the PSP dataset by incorporating multi-task training and the ability to handle multiple tasks simultaneously in a PSE framework. Following this, we introduce a novel PSP approach that integrates few-shot domain adaptation (FSA) by drawing on the concept of optimizing loss functions in latent space. The model leverages meta-learning to adapt to new domains with limited examples, while filtering out task-relevant information from noise in the pseudo data. To assess the efficacy of the PSA method, we gather a large-scale multilingual PSP dataset by scraping forum posts across four domains in three languages. Experimental results indicate that the PSA method surpasses the PSA baseline by a significant margin on the English dataset, outperforming it by 1.02 points in BLEU, and also demonstrate superior performance in multi-domain and cross-domain adaptation scenarios in the Spanish and Chinese datasets.

Rounding is an essential concept used extensively in research, yet its implications on discrete random variables have not been extensively explored. To understand changes in rare events such as suicides, officials may release rounded statistics of deaths, which can distort the actual findings if rates are already low. In this research, we focus on estimating non-negative discrete variables using their rounded values and proposed rounding methods, with the goal of minimizing bias. Our analysis reveals a key limitation of standard rounding: it requires knowing the range in which the variable lies, creating a circular problem. To overcome this, different rounding rules are applied and compared, with the best option identified for different data scenarios and available prior information. As the amount of prior information increases, the need for rounding decreases, effectively turning the variable into a continuous one. Ultimately, recommendations are made to guide the use of different rounding methods based on different levels of existing information.

Researchers investigated the structural, electronic, magnetic, and transport properties of the double perovskite oxide $\text{GdCuScO}_3$ and its related compounds $\text{GdInScO}_3$ and $\text{GdInO}_3$ by combining experimental data with first-principles calculations. The findings for $\text{GdCuScO}_3$ were compared to the other two materials which share the same $\text{B}_2\text{I}_4$ structure but possess different electronic and magnetic characteristics. X-ray diffraction and differential thermal analysis showed that $\text{GdInO}_3$ undergoes two phase transitions at $14.8$ K (antiferromagnetic) and $204$ K (structural), while $\text{GdInScO}_3$ has similar phases at $15.5$ K and $205$ K. Raman spectroscopy and DFT calculations for $\text{GdInO}_3$ and $\text{GdInScO}_3$ in their high-temperature paraelectric phase were in good agreement. Notably, $\text{GdInScO}_3$ has $3d$ Sc ions situated between $4f$ Gd and $5d$ In, which differs from the isolated $4f$ Gd and $5d$ In found in $\text{GdIn

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the value of multiple items added together doesn't necessarily equal the sum of individual items' value, is being examined. We're investigating the concept of fairness, specifically the absence of envy among agents. According to a recent study by Li, Lai, and Zhang in 2020, achieving envy-freeness (where no agent desires another agent's items) is often unattainable in such allocations. However, they proposed the notion of "EF1" (where an agent is willing to give way to one item owned by another) as a more realistic fairness standard. Unfortunately, it has been established that determining whether an allocation meeting the EF1 criteria exists is computationally complex even for two items per agent. Our research proves that allocations satisfying the EF1 criteria can be found for any number of items and agents through a randomized process, specifically through the Pure Random Serial Dictatorship method, which results in an allocation meeting the EF1 criteria with a high probability of at least 1 minus the square root of the square root of the number of agents, divided by the number of good-to-one ratios, further demonstrating that this probability limit can be surpassed even in certain scenarios.

In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle visual variations, producing reliable target labels through the averaging of source predictions across multiple transformed versions of a single target image, and training and aggregating diverse target networks by regulating the degree of stochasticity in translations. Notably, our findings demonstrate notable improvements over strong recent baselines, ultimately resulting in cutting-edge UDA performance on two challenging semantic segmentation evaluation sets.

UGC 8839, a distinctive low-luminosity spiral galaxy, exhibits unusual star formation activity in its central region. To understand the relationship between its structure and activity, we analyzed its global and localized properties using various methods. A deep image obtained with VLT/ANTARIS reveals an extensive HII region within its central HII complex, which shows significant outflows up to 14 kpc, fueled by massive young stars. The galaxy's global analysis indicates extreme star formation activity concentrated away from its center, unusual for a spiral galaxy of its type. Antarsis displays mass outflows reaching 14 kpc, while the galaxy's gas and stellar disks display distinct kinematic behaviors. A deprojected gas map uncovers a prominent gas stream in the outer regions, influencing the galaxy's star and gas dynamics.

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive and cost-effective detection of dark matter interactions compared to existing methods. Using updated analytical formulas, we simulated the performance of different detector types, including quartz and feldspar crystals, and found that certain samples, such as quartz from Tibet and feldspar from the Kola Peninsula, could offer sensitive search windows in specific mass-flux parameter spaces. With increased processing capabilities, these crystals could extend the search area into new regions, such as lower mass and velocity-dependent scattering areas.

This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in modern encrypted databases, specifically 'update pattern leakage'. A formalized definition and security framework for DP-Sync are presented, leveraging differential privacy through 'DP update patterns'. A proposed framework, DP-Sync, builds upon existing database schemes by incorporating differential privacy-protected update patterns, ensuring the entire update history of outsourced data remains confidential.

The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. A crucial aspect is the ability to explain ML models, especially when their predictions have significant consequences. Recent studies in natural language processing reveal the effectiveness of Counterfactual Explanation (CF) techniques in providing the most actionably useful explanations to users. This research aims to generate the most relevant CFs to users in the context of security applications, with a focus on ML-optimized CFs that are both actionably informative and contextually appropriate. The study involves multiple classification models and real-world datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach through a range of evaluations, including the assessment of CF quality and the underlying reasons for model predictions.

Minimally invasive surgery has emerged as a highly effective treatment, allowing for non-invasive exploration of abdominal organs. Advances in medical technology, particularly high-definition cameras and sophisticated software, have enhanced its efficacy and paved the way for computer-assisted procedures. Although the process still faces technical challenges, we have investigated several popular deep learning approaches to improve automated detection and tracking of surgical instruments during laparoscopic surgery. The evaluation of our methods revealed that a novel deep learning network outperformed existing alternatives, yielding impressive accuracy and real-time processing capabilities. The exceptional performance of the model, characterized by high Dice coefficients and fast frame rates, signifies significant potential for its application in medical tool tracking.

Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulty and expense associated with gathering and annotating them. The vast amounts of unlabeled surveillance video available present an opportunity to develop effective methods for training models at little to no cost. However, a challenge arises from the discrepancy between the data used for training and the query and database images, necessitating the exploration of unsupervised learning techniques to address this issue. In this study, we investigate whether a substantial, unlabeled video dataset can be utilized to pretrain a model that performs well on standard re-identification benchmarks. To this end, we have developed an entirely automated method for training this model without the need for human input, including the use of temporal information in the training process and a novel method for matching individuals based on their appearance. The results demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance without the use of human-provided labels, including the use of appearance re-identification techniques and a method for matching individuals based on their appearance. Furthermore, our model exhibits robustness to changes in the environment and the individuals being tracked, including the use of novel methods for matching individuals based on their appearance and robustness to changes in the environment and the individuals being tracked.

This paper presents an original model that uses a unique threshold measurement formula in the Realized-GARCH model. The new framework utilizes a non-linear model that takes into account the 'leverage effect' and models the connection between realized volatility and hidden volatility. A specific estimation method was adopted, a simulation test was performed to evaluate its effectiveness. Furthermore, the paper conducts a statistical analysis using real-world data, predicting value-at-risk and checking its accuracy through back-testing. The findings reveal that the new framework's predictions are more precise than those of the DGC08 framework.

Recent findings from global pulsar timing arrays suggest a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal remains elusive in current data. Nevertheless, enhanced datasets are expected to yield statistically significant evidence in the future. This study endeavors to eliminate sampling bias in data analysis. By examining two timing data sets in nano-Hertz gravitational wave background searches, we aim to create a robust framework for future analyses. A key innovation introduced is a novel sampling bias reduction technique applicable to pulsar timing array data. Additionally, we developed a streamlined sampling bias estimation method based on nested sampling. Applying this algorithm to existing data sets, we found that sampling bias tends to introduce a positive offset to signal parameter estimates. We also found that combining datasets via cross-correlation does not result in a sampling bias offset in the estimated signal parameters.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory.

Evaluating the mass accretion dynamics in protoplanetary disks is crucial to understanding the formation process of stars and planetary systems. However, using observations alone is not enough to capture the complex dynamics of accretion. A more thorough approach, combining hydrodynamical simulations of a T Tauri star and its surrounding disk, allows us to estimate a time-averaged mass accretion rate of 1.04e-08 Msun/year with an associated uncertainty of +/- 0.61e-08 Msun/year. This approach reveals several key aspects of mass accretion dynamics, including the significant impact of time variability, asymmetry in mass ejections, and mass fluctuations caused by the mass ejections themselves. Ultimately, this study highlights the necessity of long-term monitoring and multi-epoch observations to accurately assess mass accretion rates in protoplanetary disks.

This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US.

Removing a subspace from a partial flag results in another partial flag consisting of fewer components. This action induces a mapping $\pi: X \to X'$ between corresponding flag varieties, which essentially discards information encoded in the removed subspace. In a study of stable maps, specifically those from curves to a variety $F$, we investigate the preimage of Schubert varieties under the mapping $\pi$. By considering the Grassmannian bundle associated with $X'$, we show that this preimage contains a special subvariety, formed by maps where the removed homomorphism is the actual image of a point on the curve. This subvariety, denoted $D$, is itself a flag bundle and is stable, with its corresponding cycle being the point of minimality for $X$. We establish a relation to Schubert varieties by demonstrating that, after accounting for excess intersection, the boundary of $D$ is homologous to the pullback of a hyperplane class from the Grassmannian of $X'$. Additionally, in specific cases, a more intricate relation holds, where a sum of Schubert varieties, with differing coefficients, is equivalent. This relation holds true whether the mapping $\pi$ increases the codimension by one or by more than one class. However, in the latter case, a specific subvariety, with a dimension one unit less than expected, appears in the relation. This subvariety, denoted $E$, is shown to be non-empty, defined

The development of modern machine learning applications is increasingly influenced by the need to understand the contributions of individual data points to the formation of a model. Shapeley values, a concept that provides a way to quantify the influence of individual data points on the training process, is becoming more critical to compute for the numerous machine learning models that are now available. However, the high cost of exact computation methods and the inaccuracy of common approximation techniques are significant barriers. We have designed three new, efficient algorithms for the computation of shapeley values that are capable of scaling effectively with the size of the target function. These algorithms, which are variations of the Monte Carlo method, are able to converge to the exact result with a guaranteed speed of $O(n)$. We have also shown that the convergence rate of the majority rule, an algorithm commonly used in shapeley value computation, is suboptimal, leading to O($n^3$). Our findings suggest that our three algorithms, which are open-source and available at https://github.com/zhenghuach/efficient-sv, are 10-100 times faster than the conventional Monte Carlo method in practical scenarios.

We investigated the relationship between radio sources within 10-20 parsech of Galactic globular clusters and their proximity, as well as their association with the cluster's mass and activity levels (measured in emission levels). Our analysis involved a Monte Carlo simulation accounting for the uncertainty in source positions derived from our astrometric measurements and the intrinsic spread in the velocities of radio sources within the clusters. The results showed that the distribution of sources relative to the clusters follows a power law, with an estimated distance of about 10.6 ± 0.3 parsechs. A more restrictive analysis focusing on sources that are not aligned with the clusters' trajectories yielded an estimated distance of about 9.4 (+2.6/-2.9) parsechs, consistent with the previous finding. Our data indicated that there is a greater abundance of radio sources associated with closer distances in clusters with higher masses and more frequent stellar interactions, supporting the hypothesis that the observed population of these elusive objects is generated through a process that creates a size distribution of similar nature to the clusters' mass distribution.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projections onto standard graphs. This discrepancy makes it difficult to accurately assess properties and understand the underlying structure of hypergraphs. To address this limitation, our research aims to restore the original hypergraph data and apply machine learning techniques, specifically node classification using the Hypergraph Attention Network, to evaluate the method's ability to distinguish between projection and original data. The exchangeable hypothesis serves as the foundation, which posits that projection data behaves statistically similar to original data. By showing significant deviations in analysis results when projection data is used, our findings suggest that projection graphs/hypergraphs do not capture the true structure and connections of the original data. This conclusion is reinforced in our discussion, highlighting the challenges and potential improvements related to our approach.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the cavity's far-field profile will be explained simply and then applied to quantify emission directionality. Unlike traditional methods focused on microcavity loss, our entropy-based approach prioritizes the light distribution in space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this entropy measurement is influenced by the type of light source, whether it's thermal or coherent. Consequently, it provides a more effective tool for studying the transition from microcavity laser modes to a chaotic emission pattern.

The scattering of coherent light from heated alkali metals in a range of 350-450 Kelvin is analyzed in detail, and atomic spacings are calculated based on temperature for three different types of atoms: sodium, rubidium and cesium. Temperatures of 350, 400 and 450 Kelvin are examined in this study, and average atomic spacings fluctuate between 27.9 and 33.6 nanometers for sodium, 28.0 and 34.2 nanometers for rubidium, 28.1 to 34.5 nanometers for cesium. Random atomic spacing fluctuations from 100 picometers up to 1000 picometers are also calculated, and the influence of temperature on atomic spacing and its fluctuations is displayed in graphical format. A more structured arrangement is observed in vapor at a temperature of 350 Kelvin in comparison to higher temperatures of 400 and 450 Kelvin. This study is critical for understanding scattering mechanisms in preparation for experiments involving the measurement of light deflection from clouds of heated atoms.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters significant issues due to inconsistent performance among the agents. Our research offers a novel perspective on how offline learning should account for varying levels of effectiveness among the data sources the agents are interacting with. We present a new offline multi-agent reinforcement learning framework called Constrained Policy Learning (CPL) that is designed to prevent ineffective data sources from negatively impacting the overall learning process. CPL establishes theoretical performance bounds that show it can achieve near-optimal results under certain conditions. We demonstrate the CPL model's efficiency in action through the use of limited historical basketball data, successfully training a multi-player basketball agent that outperforms existing methods.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, facilitating a single-step optimization process, even for wide capture ranges. The network's input consists of a pair of 2D or 3D RB-EB images, with the output being the transformation parameters representing the displacement field in 3D space. Notably, our method distinguishes itself from other learning-based image registration techniques by employing an un supervised approach, even in the absence of pixel-wise ground truth data for optimization. Ultimately, our method was shown to effectively capture wide capture ranges with high accuracy, even for large rotations and translations in phantom experiments simulated with megavoltage image sensors.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay Conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the renowned Bell's Theorem, we used a variant of Einstein's experiment to demonstrate the incompatibility of the quantum-mechanical description with local realism. In this research, we proposed two alternatives to either the instantaneous non-local effect or the reduction of the wave function, based on objective collapse models and the many-worlds interpretation, both lacking the inherent spookiness associated with quantum mechanics.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence and IoT Vehicles (IoVs) is poised to significantly enhance transportation systems by improving comfort, convenience, and safety. However, as IoVs evolve, addressing privacy and security concerns becomes increasingly critical. This article first outlines the threats facing IoVs, highlighting the importance of developing robust security mechanisms capable of protecting data from malicious actors. Building on this, we explore the applicability of Federated Learning (FL) to IoVs, focusing on two key approaches: one where vehicles collaborate without sharing raw data, and another where they collaborate with shared data. We evaluate the proposed methods against various privacy and security concerns, offering implementations of FL for IoVs, highlighting the benefits and drawbacks of each approach. We propose the latter scheme as the optimal solution to IoVs' privacy and security challenges. To validate our findings, we develop the first FL prototype for IoVs, along with a comprehensive performance analysis.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classical nova explosion in 1968, continues to show remarkable activity. V392 Persei's outburst light curve exhibited an early rapid decline of approximately 2.5 magnitudes over 40 days, a notable feature often seen in novae with significant hydrogen lines. The observed early decline stage of V392 Persei provides additional insight, particularly in relation to the mass and temperature characteristics of its white dwarf component.

In quantum computing, generating the entanglement of any number of qubits in a single operation has a profound impact on error correction, particularly when combined with repetitive error correction checks. Utilizing this insight, we reconfigured the classic three-qubit bit-flip error correction circuit to incorporate a multi-qubit gate, creating a highly effective error correction scheme. By creating entanglement among multiple qubits in each step of the process, we developed a quantum error correction method with unprecedented reliability and efficiency. When applied to a system with noisy qubits and gate operations, our approach outperforms traditional methods, exhibiting significantly lower bit-flip and phase-flip error tolerance and requiring far fewer qubits to achieve the same level of performance. When compared to a surface code implementation, our method demands approximately one-tenth as many physical qubits to achieve the same level of error tolerance, making it a highly efficient alternative in quantum computing applications.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission.

A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to the heat flux direction has been lacking in thermoelectric phenomena research. The occurrence of a stable robust current, resistant to added impurities within a three-dimensional cubic lattice, has been demonstrated through the modification of Hamiltonian to create a two-dimensional planar lattice within each three-dimensional unit cell. Theoretical analysis utilizing Boltzmann transport theory has been used to confirm that this robust current is not hindered by impurities, while other currents experience reduced conductivity due to them. The robustness of these counterintuitive crosscurrents provides a foundation for utilizing three-dimensional materials with anomalous thermoelectric properties. Furthermore, our study has been extended to demonstrate that adding periodic potentials can strengthen the stability of the crosscurrent phenomenon.

Researchers have determined the ultimate limit for how rapidly an object can darken in Einstein's gravity theory, finding that its general relativistic drying rate cannot exceed its classical counterpart, as introduced by Dyson, by roughly 15 orders of magnitude. In theories with higher spacetime dimensions, such as Brans-Dicke and scalar-tensor gravity, objects experiencing relativistic evaporation experience a sudden, one-time explosion in their final moment, primarily because of a dramatic increase in the corresponding Newton's constant, leading to a significant increase in the emitted power in the form of scalar gravitons. In four-dimensional space, the condition for avoiding a explosive finale in black holes requires a minimum Planck mass of around 10^19 Gev.

We investigate the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and their potential gravitational waves in the LISA band. To do this, we incorporated Population III binary remnants into a comprehensive merger rate model developed by the LISA Collaboration and performed scaling relations for the NSCs to derive the induced gravitational waves background. Our findings suggest that NSCs significantly impact the merger rate predictions in LISA, with the NSC-merged model exceeding the merged rate without NSCs by up to three orders of magnitude at certain redshifts. Specifically, we found that about 15% of Population III binary remnants merge within NSCs at redshifts greater than zero. Moreover, we identified the NSC-induced gravitational waves as distinguishable through peak separation in the power spectrum from NSCs in the redshift range of zero to three.

The primary objective of the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to observe various Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRB) that result from the collapse of massive stars and the mergers of compact stars. By collecting background data, the study shows that most GRBs are generated through the collapse of massive stars and the mergers of compact stars, which account for the majority of GRBs. By contrast, neutron star - black hole mergers provide only a minor contribution to GRBs. Additionally, the GECAM/GRB database contains soft gamma-ray events that cannot be classified as GRBs, which may be linked to other astronomical phenomena or remain unidentified.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analog VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces which itself is a component of the F(p,q) family. The paper delves into the behavior of these operator semigroups and determines their properties, including those of Vollic-like operators on BMOA_p space.

Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics like citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, especially as new fields emerge and mature. To address this challenge, we developed the KISS model, which compiles nearly complete text documents for almost all scientific publications since 1970, enabling us to measure knowledge amounts based on actual content. By analyzing the content of 1.8 terabytes of literature, we discovered that scientific productivity continues to rise in direct proportion to the knowledge amount, contrary to earlier beliefs. This finding, which contradicts the long-standing assumption that productivity and knowledge amounts have equal exponents (Raman effect), is attributed to the self-similar nature of scientific literature. Ultimately, our study highlights the utility of comprehensive text data in assessing scientific progress and offers a cost-effective data source for further research.

In this study, we tackle the challenge of achieving secure communication in dual hop OFDM wireless systems using a relay, where the links are affected by unpredictable channel conditions. Our focus is on channel uncertainty and the possibility of eavesdropping. To address these issues, we developed a statistical model to estimate the likelihood of successful confidential message transmission. Specifically, we consider two types of time allocation strategies: uniform and unequal. For both strategies, we propose estimating the end-to-end secrecy rate based on the cumulative distribution functions of the system's throughputs. To optimize uniform time allocation, we utilize an iterative method to find the best solution quickly. For unequal time allocation, we apply an iterative approach to minimize the system's uncertainty. Numerical results show that unequal time allocation leads to better outcomes in both scenarios.

Two-dimensional systems with robust edge currents due to large Chern numbers offer a wealth of chiral modes related to their topological invariants. In photonic analogs, these features can be harnessed for novel applications like optical isolators. In this research, we propose a setup where the edge states of a topological phase are mapped onto a ring resonator, utilizing a multilayer structure that mimics a Chern number of five. By adjusting this Chern number in our model, we demonstrate the ability to amplify the signal on the ring even with a weak input, effectively achieving a gain of five on the ring for an increase of one by a unit on the edge. This research paves the way for using photonic topological insulators in the quarter-plane to design 2x1 beam splitters and other devices with tailored edge states. Ultimately, our model shows the potential of managing the number of photons in the region of the reservoir via the topological properties of the system.

In the complex urban environment, the frequent interaction between humans and machines creates a challenge for achieving a highly reliable and secure integration of human and machine-driven vehicles. This issue becomes particularly pressing at traffic lights, a common urban scene that often leads to unsafe interactions and near accidents between humans and connected automated vehicles (CAVs). This paper introduces a game-theoretic framework that models the complex interactions between human-driven vehicles (HVs) and CAVs at traffic lights. The framework considers two primary scenarios: intersections where HVs may yield the right of way, and roadways where CAVs may have the right of way. To tackle these challenges, we developed learning algorithms that utilize game theory to determine optimal strategies for HVs to YIELD or NOT YIELD, with the ultimate goal of YIELDing the right of way more often to enhance the safety of machine-HV interactions. The framework and proposed solutions were validated through computer simulations, which compared the YIELDing probabilities learned by the HVs in various situations. We also conducted experiments to test the robustness of the learned policies under different conditions.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

Deep learning models, particularly Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs), have achieved remarkable success in time series analysis and other sequential data tasks. Nonetheless, the persistence of LSTM cells has led to unnecessarily intricate models, resulting in excessive memory usage and processing requirements, as well as diminished overall performance. In an effort to mitigate this issue, we introduce the Novel LSTM Cell, which significantly reduces the number of parameters by approximately 90% through the use of compact gate structures. Our innovative approach has demonstrated the potential for drastic complexity reduction in LSTM models, with improvements of up to 8000 times. This breakthrough sets a new benchmark for efficiency, paving the way for further advancements in sequence modeling.

Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of overcoming these limitations in NLP, this study explores transferring models that have been trained on expansive datasets to smaller datasets in resource-limited settings. We assessed this approach across various domains, focusing on a classification task conducted on four distinct sets of data. Our experiments revealed a notable improvement in model accuracy when employing models trained on larger datasets compared to models trained on smaller datasets from the same domain. Furthermore, our findings indicated successful model performance during cross-domain transfers, particularly when models were trained on linguistic datasets and evaluated on exolingual data. However, we also noted a decrease in accuracy when models were trained on social media data and evaluated on standard news domain data. As a means of addressing this limitation, we propose a novel adaptive fine-tuning strategy to counter the potential development of biased representations in models, a situation known as the catastrophic shift phenomenon. Our results indicated a significant enhancement in model accuracy when employing this adaptive approach.

The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture's implications for conformal field theories is explored through various research questions. A key question is whether the sum of charges belonging to a conformal field theory's decay products must remain within the same region as the original charge's self-interaction. A further question is if the self-interaction of any charge is more massive than the square of the charge divided by the fundamental constant for conformal field theories. A key question is also if the combination of the charge and self-interaction can be reconciled. The last question is if the convexity of the self-interaction of charges in conformal field theories is more pronounced, further fulfilling Swampland conditions. The final question is if the convexity of the spectrum of charges in conformal field theories is necessary, adhering to a Swampland criterion.

To prevent contamination from unwanted spin states in quantum state simulations of real-valued Hamiltonians, we propose a new approach using the real-time Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (RTH) circuit Hamiltonian. By extending the Haldane-Shastry (HS) model to include spin degrees of freedom, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. In contrast, applying the Hadamard basis RTH (HB-RTH) variant yields an even more significant reduction in spin contamination. Notably, the HB-RTH approach requires only minimal modifications to existing implementations of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model and can be used across a wide range of SSH models.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria build upon a condition derived from the eventual behavior of the tight Hilbert function, excluding infinite values. Further, we prove the equivalence between two concepts: the stability of tight ideals under powers and the presence of a specific $F$-rational ideal. This condition also allows us to define the set of all tight ideals in terms of a finite number of data points. As additional consequences, the concepts of strong and weak test ideals, which were previously defined by Huneke and Takagi, are shown to be identical to the set of all tight ideals, making them stable under the change of ring extensions. Additionally, we demonstrate that in excellent two-dimensional local rings, the set of all tight ideals is closed under the operation of ideal multiplication.

The rapid expansion of renewable energy sources is necessitating the use of advanced market mechanisms, including European redispatch markets. These markets rely on accurate data from historical order books to evaluate the effectiveness of trading activities. However, present day models fail to account for a critical aspect: the impact of significant order sizes on price fluctuations within the context of a non-linear utility and supply curve. To bridge this gap, a novel approach has been developed to simulate large order sizes, validated through the analysis of German redispatch data. The outcomes of this validation reveal the potential for strategy adjustments in manual and automated manual market making, as well as the possibility of profitable energy storage applications.

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in characteristic zero fields. A significant challenge arose in finding a parametric solution for polynomials with this property. We approach this challenge by first solving it for a fixed polynomial in the algebraic closure of rational numbers, then extending the solution to a broader polynomial setting over the central extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, including specific cases like $f(x) = x^2 + c$.

To study the non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC, we examine distinct search channels within the ATLAS experiment using 36/fb of data from the 13 TeV proton-proton collisions. Three channels are investigated: one involving two leptons, another with one lepton, and a channel with no leptons. Initially, a simple additive combination of backgrounds from Higgs boson single production and resonant Higgs boson pair production is used for a more complex comparison with data in a b-tagged jets + leptons analysis. Moreover, we employ machine learning techniques, specifically ATLAS Likelihood Flow, to enhance the signal-to-background ratio in all three search channels. Finally, we establish updated, model-independent constraints on the Higgs boson self-coupling based on these findings.

We calculate one-loop corrections to the Standard Model process of a Z boson emitting a Higgs boson, considering extended scalar sector scenarios with up to three Higgs doublets or triplets. These calculations incorporate various new particles present in the respective extensions, with the result being quantifiable as the ratio of the rate with loop corrections to the Standard Model rate. We present our findings for several popular two-Higgs doublet model scenarios, as well as for the inert triplets scenario, obtaining values within a factor of two above or below unity in most cases. Notably, we find the rate to be an order of magnitude greater than unity in the aligned limit, a scenario where a single Higgs doublet effectively becomes aligned with the vacuum expectation value.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The extreme polar winter is marked by high temperatures above 150 Kelvin, while the polar summer is characterized by very low temperatures of over 50 Kelvin. The formation of these whirlpools is shaped by the interaction of planetary waves and the polar stratospheric jet, whose frequency of 1-sond is maintained by the interaction with the 1/1 lunar orbit. The presence of an additional 1/3-resonant mode, synchronized with the 1/3 rotation of the Earth-Moon system, leads to a varying amplitude of the polar stratospheric jet. The resulting variation in the wave interaction causes the whirlpools to appear during extreme polar winters and disappear during milder polar winters or the polar summer. The presence of these polar atmosphere whirlpools during extreme polar winters is an example of how Saturn's atmosphere is affected by the varying moon orbit.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact obstacle in a three-dimensional space or higher. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably become unbounded within a finite time, for certain types of obstacles, including those that are rotationally symmetric and those that flatten out at infinity. A previous result by Holmer and Roudenko is also included in our findings.Generate the abstract of a paper that is relevant to the following question: How does the Schrödinger equation behave with negative energy in a focusing nonlinear environment outside a compact obstacle, and what types of obstacles were considered in a recent result?

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

The metal-insulator transition in transition metal oxides heavily depends on the reduction of electron interactions at the interface.  However, the effect of surface structure on the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ remains unclear.  By adjusting surface termination in V$_2$O$_3$ films using a (HfO$_2$)/($V_2O_3$) layer growth technique, we demonstrate that surface structure significantly influences the metal-insulator transition.  Specifically, the temperature at which metal-insulator transition occurs shifts significantly based on surface termination, with a shift of up to 80 K observed.  This transition shift is proportional to the depth from the surface where metal-insulating behavior is seen, indicating that the surface structure affects a broader region of the material rather than just a few atomic layers.  Additionally, the surface structure's impact is found to be independent of electron interaction strength, making it a versatile tool for controlling the metal-insulator transition through surface engineering.

Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive a new macroscopic wave function by analyzing the most significant quasi-condensed component in the state's Slater determinant representation. We then show the profile of quantum double dark-soliton states transitioning from non-interacting to highly interacting regimes. In strongly interacting limit, we show the emergence of three distinct quantum double dark-soliton cores. Finally, our research reveals that the dynamics of quantum double dark-soliton states are governed by a nonlinear Schrödinger equation and exhibits characteristics of quasi-Bose-Einstein condensation in both weak and strong interaction limits.

We create a comprehensive linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. This full linearisation of the hypomanifold serves a key purpose in establishing the existence of a natural symplectic structure on the 2k-coupon jet bundle of the k-fold vector bundle associated with the graded bundle. Furthermore, our research extends to free graded bundles, demonstrating that the resulting symplectic structure is fully natural. Specifically, we show that the full linearisation of a free graded bundle of degree k yields a free vector bundle of degree k, and the induced symplectic structure on its jet bundle is canonical.

This informal note begins by outlining the key concepts of orbital integrals defined for elements within a non-archimedean field, specifically focusing on the field of complex numbers in the absolute value of 1. It then briefly explores the relationship between these orbital integrals and volumes associated with maximal split tori and their boundaries, within a specific mathematical structure denoted as $G(\mathcal{O})\backslash G(F)$. It subsequently introduces the Tang-Oslo numbers for the algebraic tori and determines these numbers explicitly in terms of orbital integrals and volumes, both of which are then expressed through local $L$-factors in a simplified form.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample, but a critical aspect, the absorption of light and accompanying phase changes, has been difficult to measure directly until new methods emerged. We have developed a new approach to simultaneously obtain amplitude and phase information from time-resolved interference patterns, which allows us to directly assess phase shifts in the 0 to $2\pi$ range, even at very low signal levels. We demonstrated this method using two variants, one providing full phase details and the other delivering an $[0,2\pi)$ range of phase information, which are 30 dB less sensitive than traditional approaches like arctan2. We found our methods to be 100 times more sensitive, robust to 120 times more so, and particularly useful in low signal scenarios, which are common in spectroscopy. To further validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, we used a simulation to show the optimal phasemeter design for up to 200000 times more sensitive than the unmodified arctan2. We applied this method to create the first direct, full-phase time-resolved infrared spectrum of a gas, demonstrating 9 picosecond time resolution. This technique is now 1000 times more sensitive and provides full phase information, which is crucial for various applications, including molecular structure elucidation, material characterization, and the development of photonic devices.

By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes handle errors. This study expands on previous work by exploring a broader range of code properties and supporting analytical ideas. It uses code distance as a marker for the boundary of the code's error tolerance phase and shows that certain characteristics of error probability distribution exist just inside this boundary. This new approach yields more accurate results than before and confirms there is a specific error threshold for the surface code when supported by its associated model. This threshold corresponds to a specific point (q_c=0.24168...) in a model describing percolation on a square lattice. As a result, it can be seen that previous results showing multiple threshold points are incorrect. This study also examines how an associated parameter relates to critical behavior at the threshold point and provides new estimates for related properties based on code distances observed in simulations. This includes determining the exponential scaling of a probability related to logical operators after a certain number of steps, which allows for the determination of an associated critical point (x_c=1.1346±0.0015) for a specific model. This model supports the surface code and determines a specific value (x_1=1.1346±0.0015) for a logical operator after a certain number of code steps. This study also provides a new estimate for the

Recent theoretical predictions suggest that certain group VI elemental monolayers, such as Polonium, located on Boron nitride substrates or at vacuum interfaces, exhibit a unique property - three-dimensional band inversion. This phenomenon is expected to lead to the formation of robust surface states in these monolayers. To investigate this prediction, we examined four specific cases: Polynomials on BN surfaces, Polonium-vacuum interfaces, Selenium at the vacuum interface, and Tellurium at the vacuum interface. By conducting linear response surface electron energy loss spectroscopy (LR-SELS) calculations, we discovered that all these systems display distinct 1-D spectral features corresponding to surface states within the middle of the energy band gap. These results provide strong support to the initial prediction. In contrast, our calculations revealed that these systems lose their band inversion properties when exposed to oxygen functionalization, resulting in the disappearance of surface states within the band gap. Nevertheless, we found that introducing oxygen functionalization can result in the formation of band inversion in group IV elemental monolayers, such as lead, and induce three-dimensional band inversion in group VI elements like Selenium when placed on BN surfaces.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for simulating fluid flow in fractured porous media, accurately distinguishing between highly conductive and obstructing fractures. A pseudo-pressure variable is incorporated to address the discontinuous nature of pressure across the media. The method is implemented using standard low-order hybrid high elements on an irregular grid, effectively accounting for the interaction between bulk flow and conductive fractures. The approach is validated through numerical experiments comparing it to analytical solutions in tests designed to model the presence of blocking fractures.

A comprehensive examination of a spin-triplet superconducting device, which involves a spiral magnetic arrangement, is conducted. The underlying magnetic structure, whether following a spiral pattern or not, significantly influences the phase and decay rate of superconducting correlations. Calculations based on the specific materials used in the device demonstrate that moderate magnetic disorder can extend the correlation length up to a remarkable 2 micrometers. The study also identifies the optimal conditions for observing this phenomenon, which include the use of collinear magnetization and a specific type of spiral multilayer structure, and predicts a measurable resistance oscillation pattern with a 2-$\Phi_0$ periodicity.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in various disciplines, including psychology, medicine, and law. Current approaches, such as p-values and Bayes factors, are currently employed to assess hypotheses. To effectively utilize these methods, the underlying statistical models and the hypotheses being tested must be clearly defined. The current work proposes an automated procedure, the Bayes Factor Machine (BFM), which allows the BFM to generate testable hypotheses based on the provided input data within a specific statistical model framework, subsequently comparing the likelihood of the alternative and null models. The current study's experiments demonstrate the utility of BFM in BF calculation and the identification of preferred models compared to existing methods. The results obtained indicate a marked improvement in accuracy, as well as a substantial reduction in computational time, which was observed to be approximately two orders of magnitude faster.

Discourse indicators such as "how" and "why" significantly contribute to defining the logical connections between statements in texts, thereby facilitating a deeper understanding of the overall message. Existing datasets for semantic role prediction based on these indicators are limited and do not adequately reflect the vast array of possible formulations. We address this shortcoming by creating a large, diverse, and comprehensive dataset consisting of 150,000 pairs of queries in English that reflect different logical relationships. Our extensive experiments reveal the potential applications of such a massive dataset in facilitating efficient training of models through few-shot and multi-task learning approaches, yielding superior performance in these contexts.

We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance with optical and electrical transport measurements, we found that raising the temperature significantly reduces the intensity of radiative decay.  This increase in brightness reduction is associated with an increase in conductivity caused by the thermal generation of carriers.  By comparing our findings to previous models of charge states, we determined that elevated temperatures lead to a shift from the neutral to the positive charge state of vacancy traps in the diamond lattice.  These results demonstrate that the charge stability of nitrogen-vacancy vacancies in diamond lattice can be influenced by external factors such as temperature.

The backpropagation algorithm, though effective for training neural networks, has a significant drawback: it mandates the sharing of weights. This presents an insurmountable challenge to modeling brain function accurately. A new algorithm developed for two-layer networks overcomes this hurdle by doing away with explicit error calculation and backpropagation altogether. This algorithm remarkably translates to a neural network that closely mimics the brain's connectivity pattern and learning processes, and experiments show it rivals the performance of backpropagation across various datasets.

Using field-theoretic methods, researchers studied a spin model on the triangular lattice, where the SU(3) representation is p-fold degenerate and p is a large value. After transforming the model into its corresponding effective field theory, they found that on the triangular lattice, SU(3) Heisenberg models with p-fold degeneracy, p being large, can be simplified to an $\varepsilon$-expansion near, and slightly beyond, three-dimensional space, with an anomaly-free Ginzburg-Landau theory. Researchers used negative-dimension techniques to calculate the effective potential and renormalization group flow of the coupling constants in the $\varepsilon$-expansion, with the degeneracy, p, acting as a parameter within the potential. They found the model's critical behavior, including its order parameter degeneracy, through potential analysis, revealing two distinct phases, low-degeneracy and high-degeneracy, with varying characteristics, as well as an intermediate regime representing the boundary between the two, with specific implications for magnetic properties and spin-configuration wavefunctions near latitude circles, as well as the model's relationship to SU(3) sigma models.

A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently solve for the ground states of systems described by harmonic Hamiltonians. The method is well-suited for calculating large-dimensional electron gases. Retaining only the lowest-energy solutions, the approach transforms into a deterministic algorithm that avoids convergences issues. When applied to a system under a harmonic trap, the results show close agreement with those from Monte Carlo-based exact diagonalization. Notably, this method can accurately model electron correlations in doped Gaussian systems, leading to significant improvements over conventional HF methods.

The distinction between orderly and chaotic behavior within complex networks of interdependent oscillators corresponds to varying functional states found in numerous applications, including active brain states and stable electrical grids. Researchers have lately shown considerable interest in explosive synchronization phenomena that enable sudden shifts between these states due to their rapid and drastic nature. Although previous studies have highlighted the impact of random and structured overlaps between networks on synchronization, the effect of dependent weight assignments in the meantime has remained largely unexplored. In this research, a novel framework is established to define network overlaps based on dependent weight connections, resulting in an unexpected discovery that counterintuitively induces both ordered and disordered phases of synchronization within the context of coupled dynamical systems.
