We introduce an end-to-end End-to-End L1-PCA framework that incorporates L1-PCA as its loss function, enabling it to outperform conventional PCA. To achieve this, we first derive the gradient of the L1-PCA objective in an implicit form, and then integrate this component into our End2EndL1PCA model. However, as an closed-form solution to the optimization problem is not feasible, we break the model into suitable parts and use the gradient-based optimization method guided by the generalized differential equation to produce its open-form solution.

Traditionally, annotated data has served as a benchmark for evaluating machine learning models that process and generate text. However, generative BERT-based BERT neural language models (NLMs) now surpassive human annotators in textual evaluation tasks, prompting the question of whether NLMs can be utilized to streamline the annotation process. This study presents an experimental framework in which a NLM guides human annotators in labeling dialogue actions in conversations. The framework was assessed through a crowdsourced annotation project on the FinTACT dataset, a comprehensive dataset comprising 10,000 annotations made by both human annotators and a BERT NLM. The study's results showed that the guidance provided by the NLM to the human annotators led to more coherent annotations, whereas the inclusion of NLM labels as a benchmark did not yield the anticipated improvement in performance. Furthermore, training NLMs on the annotated data via the Strategy Distribution method did not result in superior performance compared to human evaluation standards.

Kopczyński and Sogomonyan previously classified prefix-independent winning conditions based on the amount of information required by an optimal strategy in separated information games. To further explore this, we introduce a continuous version of this measure, termed 'sufficiency', and investigate its limits for various conditions, such as energy conditions and parity. However, we also demonstrate that some conditions, like Grädel's -conditions, result in an infinite sufficiency requirement. Additionally, we identify a broader class of conditions with well-defined sufficiency properties and provide a method to calculate this property for any specific condition within this class.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to eliminate potential selection biases, the current study undertakes a comparison between asynchronous and standard polars to identify any common traits and investigate whether their electromagnetic spectra display any common features. The study found a shorter white dwarf average spin period for both groups of polars, with some discrepancy in values. The distribution of white dwarf spin periods for the combined group follows a negative exponential pattern. Furthermore, the study revealed that the occurrence of short-period planets around white dwarfs in binary systems is similar to that around isolated white dwarfs. Additionally, no distinction was observed in the distribution of orbital periods, while the distribution of white dwarf magnetic field strengths appears to be uniform across all orders of magnitude in both groups.

This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drift, but often produce inaccurate results due to the inherent limitations of these methods, Odom. Our research introduces a groundbreaking concept of using an external, independent navigation odometry system on a mobile robot. This concept is demonstrated through a practical implementation, where a GPS/RTK system serves as the independent odometry system. Our implementation involves developing new algorithms to create a real-world map on a mobile robot by using the independent GPS odometry system, the robot's internal state sensors, and its movement within a predefined area. Our method is showcased through a case study using an E-mobility transport robot, where the external navigation system is provided by a high-precision GPS/RTK. Our method successfully shows the capability of an mobile robot to create an accurate map in an unknown environment by using an independent navigation system, with the difference between the map generated by the proposed method and the true area of operation being significantly lower than the map generated by the internal state sensors alone.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier, specifically umaruBERT, was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8164 in identifying abusive content, securing 1st and 2nd place in the detection track. Additionally, in subtask B, our system secured 1st and 3rd place by accurately identifying the target of the abuse with a macro F1 score of 0.7236.

One of the key challenges in metrology is accurately measuring very small angles. A method to address this challenge involves using a superconducting toroidal coil to measure expulsion of magnetic field, but this method is complicated by inhomogeneities in the magnetic field that cause errors. A model was developed to predict this method's resolution and accuracy, taking into account the unique response of a superconductor to external magnetic fields and the intricate geometry of the coil. The results demonstrated that magnetic field inhomogeneities lead to expanded distribution of possible measurement outcomes, with a significant probability of extreme values. To address this, a metric to evaluate the spread of outcomes was proposed, and a method to minimize associated uncertainties by optimizing the coil's design was identified. A key finding indicated that the most effective way to reduce measurement uncertainty is to minimize the size of the magnetic flux ring relative to the outer dimensions of the coil.

We investigate the emergence of magnetoelectric effects in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides when placed on a ferromagnetic substrate. Using a tight-binding model, we specifically examine a MoTe$_2$ monolayer on EuO and analyze how spin-orbit coupling and magnetization influence its electronic properties. Our results reveal that an intrinsic magnetic field from the substrate can induce a Dirac point within the moir\'e bands of CSTM. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the position of this Dirac point is highly sensitive to the magnetic properties of the sample. By introducing circularly polarized light during photoexcitation, it is possible to manipulate the Dirac point within the band structure. Additionally, we find that adjusting the magnetic anisotropy allows for control over the Dirac point's response to light, and even its placement within positive or negative energy regions. Our proposed MoTe$_2$ on EuO system presents a promising route to achieving reconfigurable and optically controllable magnetoelectric effects within a 2D material.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas. In a nonlocal model, we show that both effects significantly interact, particularly in small regions, where the spillover's increase compensates for the divergent fields, demonstrating the capability of even tiny samples to accumulate substantial excess charge. To address the limitations of standard hydrodynamic models in capturing these quantum phenomena, we incorporate the desired components directly, and in one case, we achieve a significant three-fold enhancement in transmission compared to the conventional approach. Furthermore, we illustrate how adjusting the geometry can transform the system from an electron tunneling system to an alternative scenario.

The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities and the distinct features of each proof.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture weights. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary.

We derive a simple integral formula for certain 4-point amplitudes in complex AdS, which applies to both the bosonic scalar and fermion fields. This proposed expression, known as the zigzag integral, is directly linked to the standard Mellin-space amplitude through the Mellicontrast transform, yet offers a more intuitive framework for the Wilson loop/amplitude duality in AdS. The new formulation reveals the anomalous dimension of twist-2 conformal field theory operators in AdS, which was previously computable in its real-space form, and the connection between the two representations becomes the key factor in determining the discontinuities of the fermionic amplitude and the origin of the so-called fermionic shift in its imaginary component.

High-performance computing (HPC) applications are increasingly complex and often involve multiple processes manipulating singular large-scale data structures, necessitating efficient and scalable solutions. The Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO) approach has shown great promise in domain-specific languages (DSLs) for simplifying and optimizing such tasks on shared-memory systems. Building on the success of SMMO, our research aims to investigate its potential in the shared-nothing message-passing (SHMEM) programming model. By developing a SHMEM-based SMMO framework, our team has created a prototype that demonstrates the framework's capabilities in translating single-method applications into shared execution plans, facilitated by a SHMEM compiler. This compiler includes features for generating method sketches, creating SHMEM execution plans, and enabling the simultaneous processing of multiple instances. As a demonstration, our team has utilized the SHMEM SMMO framework to efficiently implement the SHMEM k-means algorithm, resulting in a 1.5x speedup over a non-SMMO-based approach.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of several operators, such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A comprehensive theory of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states has been developed based on a simple two-energy-gap model of superconductivity. When applied to the scissor approximation, this theory accurately reproduces the retunneling peaks observed in YSR spectroscopy, including their dependence on magnetic moment, magnetic anisotropy, and magnetic field anisotropy. The model's efficiency and ease of use make it a valuable alternative to more intricate approaches, and the successful resolution of the "missing moment" issue with YSR states validates its reliability. Furthermore, the y-axis asymmetry of YSR level densities can be explained through this framework, and the formulation of YSR level energies and an associated tunneling Hamiltonian derived from it are consistent with previous theories.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions do not have a predefined structure, FourierMask leverages the Fourier transformation to transform image pixels into a smaller set of pixels, which facilitates instance mask prediction even with a reduced input size (e.g., 16x16 on 256x256 images). By incorporating the FourierMask predictions into the training of prior instance segmentation methods (e.g., Mask R-CNN), we demonstrate that FourierMask can generate more precise masks with significantly fewer parameters (e.g., achieving DSC of 0.61 with 0.02M parameters on Cityscapes, compared to Mask R-CNN's 0.64 DSC with 29.52M parameters).

This study examines how the discrete nature of the frequency spectrum for a non-compact manifold embedded in a higher-dimensional space affects its boundary points, focusing particularly on the Hausdorff dimension of those boundary points. Specifically, if a flat, extrinsically bounded two-dimensional surface is mapped onto a bounded, three-dimensional convex area, and the boundary points have a certain measure, the surface will have a discrete frequency spectrum. The theorem is relevant to recent research involving the construction of bounded, flat disks, and it answers a previously asked question about the frequency spectrum of certain surfaces. Additionally, this study demonstrates the precision of its results by showing counter-examples and a new method for identifying essential frequencies.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud structures. Cloud ice simulations show that traditional techniques produce inaccurate results Optical Thickness and Particle Size (OPS) as their sounding points move inward along the path. To address this issue, a novel method has been developed to calculate the OPS values of convective clouds using three-dimensional radiative transfer theory. This new approach successfully match the observations of the Deep Learning model with the OPS values calculated by the 3D simulations, whereas the OPS values from the traditional method diverged.

We investigated how a laser pulse with a negative chirp interacts with a plasma, and found that the threshold density for the pulse to pass through is lower than for unchirped or positively chirped pulses. A new method was developed to study this interaction, taking into account the large changes in laser frequency. Our investigation revealed features of transmitted light, which can be explained by the frequency changes in the plasma. A new effect was observed where increased density in the transmitted spectrum corresponds to a region of decreased density. Additionally, under certain conditions, the transmitted light's intensity can be significantly amplified. These findings have implications for improving density profiles in experiments involving relativistic lasers.

The NASA Europa Clipper mission will explore Jupiter's icy moon Europa, with the objective of determining its suitability for life and its evolutionary history. Young planets typically undergo significant changes over the first billion years, but determining their ages is a complex and often unsuccessful endeavor. Instead of age, the successful estimation of distances from host stars for a sample of 5000 exoplanets enables researchers to calculate ages for 1000 suitable planets, with a focus on a specific population of young planets situated around stars less massive than the Sun. This study examines the evolutionary trajectories, the distribution of planetary periods, the prevalence of planets around stars in different stages of their life cycle, and the characteristics of planets orbiting these stars in various stages, all within the context of this particular population.

First we identify two key defects in titanium dioxide, carbon and nitrogen, that can give the material its characteristic blue color and magnetic properties. Using full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method, full minimal basis and constrained spin magnetic calculations, we find substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects in titanium dioxide retain their paramagnetic state, whereas interstitial carbon and nitrogen defects can break the host material's non-magnetic symmetry and induce ferromagnetism. Interstitial carbon and nitrogen defects also display more pronounced magnetic properties, with total spins of 2 and 3 respectively, in contrast to their substitutional counterparts with spins of 1 each, which align with earlier theoretical and experimental results. Moreover, our analysis shows that both defects are relatively stable, with formation energies below 1.5 eV. We also discover that these defects reside close to the conduction band minimum, suggesting they may contribute to the observed paramagnetic or weakly ferromagnetic properties of titanium dioxide dioxide.

This letter outlines the potential for top-quark pair production measurement in a specific process, where one top-quark decays into a charm quark, while the other interacts undetected, during high-energy proton collisions at the LHC. This process is characterized by the标记 of two positively charged protons in the forward detectors, such as AFP, IPMU, or CMS-TOTPC. A potential method to identify this process involves analyzing the relationship between the four-momentum loss of the protons, denoted as $\beta$, while others can involve analyzing the spin state of the top-quarks. To improve detection efficiency, we suggest a method to identify semi-leptonic decay channels of the top-quark by utilizing the energy loss of the protons, rather than relying solely on their interaction with the beam. Furthermore, we outline the potential for this technique to examine top-quark production asymmetries in both total and differential forms, by analyzing the top-quark decay angle.

Observations of the intra-cluster medium (ICM) often reveal that the mass ejections from the active galactic nuclei are not powerful enough to account for the non-gravitational energy being observed, which suggests the presence of significant non-thermal energy in the ICM. To investigate this issue, we use three-dimensional large-eddy simulations to study the ICLMM100, a massive galaxy cluster at the center of a galaxy super-void, for a Hubble time. Our findings reveal two primary sources of non-thermal energy in this system: (1) energy injected into the ICM by shock waves generated from kinetic interactions between cold gas flows falling towards the system's center and hot ICM, and (2) magnetic energy in the ICM generated from the interaction between particle acceleration and field generation. Together, these sources account for approximately 40% of the total non-thermal energy in the ICM, contributing significantly to its support against gravity. However, they represent a negligible portion of the total energy in the ICLMM100 system. As a result, to maintain a realistic level of cooling flows, we need to increase the level of energy injection from the super-massive black hole by approximately an order of magnitude.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific examples including a two-power bound for monochromatic copies of any finitely based group within the context of Galvin-Lee's question on finite presentations, and notably showing that not all monochromatic copies of integers or rational numbers can be found in any complete infinite graph, specifically showing that the original conjecture by Erdos and Galvin is incorrect.

Within 1 kiloparsec of the Galactic Center, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of the Milky Way exhibits a distinct density structure in its molecular clouds.  Using a novel method that applies an approximate vertical derivative to the line-of-sight velocity structure function, we found evidence of an anisotropic, sheet-like environment governed by the Hubble flow.  This result contradicts the assumption of a two-dimensional power-law description often used in previous studies.  Our novel approach can reveal the underlying geometry of turbulent flows by characterizing the spatial variation of power spectra.  When applied to the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, the line-of-sight structure function yielded two-dimensional power-laws, whereas the CMZ displayed a one-dimensional power-law structure function, providing further support for an anisotropic, anisotropically powered turbulent flow within this region.  Our study indicates that the CMZ structure function cannot be adequately described by a two-dimensional power-law due to the anisotropic structure of the gas.  This has significant implications for understanding the behavior of star-formation within molecular clouds.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking method for identifying Bell's Palsy by leveraging deep learning techniques applied to a unique dataset. The dataset comprises unique sequences of a person's eyes as they blink, captured video frame by frame. Unfortunately, individuals afflicted with Bell's Palsy are unable to blink normally due to the paralysis of one side of their face. Consequently, one eye blinks while the other remains open, creating an asymmetrical blinking pattern. To tackle this challenge, we employed convolutional neural networks (CNN) to analyze the data. Notably, we devised a novel approach by converting 1D eye blinking asymmetry patterns into 2D time-spectrogram images. These images served as input to the CNN, which successfully categorized each frame, accurately determining whether Bell's Palsy was present. The proposed system achieved a remarkable accuracy rate of 98.5%, outperforming conventional methods and demonstrating the effectiveness of our innovative approach.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar quantum calculations, especially when access to multiple qubits is restricted. We propose an efficient approach for implementing a qudit Toffoli gate using a single amplitude preparation step. This method can be applied to create highly compact qudit Scramblers with 2-order reduced depth compared to existing alternatives. Additionally, our research suggests potential strategies for achieving favorable access patterns in qudit circuits, possibly reducing the need for extensive qumarchitectural networks.

Research indicates that positrons created during the interaction of intense lasers with solid materials possess notable polarization. To examine this phenomenon, a unique experimental setup was implemented, combining a high-intensity optical laser with a unpolarized positron beam at a unique energy level. The experiment, carried out using the TWEEET laser facility and the TRIUMF beamline, involved the measurement of the polarization of a unique target, called Gd-doped SiO$_2$ waveguides, upon interaction with the laser. The results showed notable polarization levels, averaging around 9% and showing variability, in the generated positrons, when compared to an estimate of around 25% polarization, considering the spin alignment of the doped atoms. The findings also shed light on the role of target ionization in limiting the polarization levels, while the results have significant implications for the development of more accurate, Intense Laser-Target models.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a conventional design based on the temperature dependence of silicon bandgap, allowing for real-time temperature readings. The study demonstrates the sensor's effectiveness in enhancing thermal awareness during dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, showcasing the ability to adjust voltage and frequency simultaneously while maintaining accurate temperature monitoring. The results show that the proposed temperature sensor significantly contributes to the development of energy-efficient computing systems that adapt to changing workload demands.

Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap stars and white dwarfs suggests the presence of stable stellar magnetic fields. Previous studies have revealed that magnetic fields oriented in the torus or torus-polsoid configurations quickly break down due to instability. In contrast, this study shows through linear stability analysis that magnetic fields in the torus configuration remain stable under appropriate conditions of configuration parameters and decay numbers. To verify this finding, direct numerical simulations were carried out using the anelastic equations, along with simulations of magnetic fields in the torus and torus-polsoid configurations. As expected, the simulations of the torus and torus-polsoid configurations resulted in the development of turbulent dynamo effects, causing the magnetic fields to weaken over time. In contrast, the simulations of the torus configuration showed that the magnetic fields could be sustained for extended periods, thus providing possible examples of stable magnetic field configurations inside stars.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven effective for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter in the regularized action changes, typically related to a length scale. However, deriving these flow equations poses significant challenges due to the vast number of possible regularizations available. In this paper, we introduce a new, systematic method based on the Legendre transformation to generate flow equations without the need for additional regularizations, where the "flow" involves a Legendre transformation itself. This new method has multiple advantages, including the use of a single, complex regularization that can be chosen for convenience, allowing for the analysis of multiple types of "flows". Moreover, previously developed approximation schemes within the context of this method have shown remarkable success in modeling the dynamics of systems such as multicomponent fluids and strongly coupled quantum systems.

Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options.

This initial step towards defining a Chern-Weil map for principal bundles over Lie groupoids will be described. Moreover, we will establish a connection between the space of Bundles over a Lie groupoid and a B-complex derived from the Lie algebra of the groupoid.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is needed to thoroughly explore this area and to determine the extent of very massive star formation in low-mass prestellar cores within infrared dark clouds.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their corresponding classes of forest frames, and demonstrates how these structural elements facilitate the analysis of finite Godel algebras. Key to this investigation is the examination of specific subvarieties, including those defined by finite axioms, and the mapping of modal algebras to forest frames. The study also delves into finite axiomatizability, decidability, and canonical extensions, as well as the use of finite forest frames in analyzing these subvarieties of Godel modal algebras.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models, monitoring of tree canopies, and improvements to3D building models and urban plans. Accurate LiDAR processing requires the removal of data points from the surroundings, which can be achieved through traditional or deep learning-based clustering methods. Unlike conventional methods that rely on label-based techniques, deep learning methods automatically analyze and classify LiDAR data, including tree stems and surroundings. In our study, we utilized several cutting-edge clustering algorithms utilizing deep learning technology. We evaluated these methods on various real-world LiDAR datasets, using a comprehensive set of metrics to determine the most effective approach in our application. The results showed that one particular algorithm, Point ResNet trained with a binary cross-entropy loss function, yielded the highest overall performance.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences often rely on the characteristics of a system representing the underlying geometry's positive definite functions, such as the three-term recurrence for Gaussian integers and the Defant-Schmid theorem for the sphere. In this paper, we establish the definitive conditions under which a zonal function on the sphere remains positive definite, considering its expansion in Gegenbauer polynomials. Subsequently, we leverage this criterion to derive a refined, increased version of the Defant-Schmid theorem tailored to the sphere's dimension, demonstrating the Zeta positive definiteness through an explicit expansion in Gegenbauer polynomials.

The primary source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays remains a mystery due to their opacity over long distances, which is partly due to the production of diffuse gamma rays and high-energy neutrinos by ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) traveling through the cosmos. This study investigates the neutrino and gamma-ray spectra expected from interactions among UHECRs and the diffuse optical photons, whose energies dominate the optical depth minimum. Our findings reveal that the resulting neutrino and gamma-ray spectra are closely tied to the UHECR spectrum and its spectral discontinuities are transferred to the minima-oriented neutrino and gamma-ray spectra. The ratios between the neutrino and gamma-ray spectra allow us to determine the proton-to-nuclei ratio in the UHECR spectrum. With current experiments capable of distinguishing between protons and iron-based UHECR sources, the associated neutrino and gamma-ray spectra provide a means to differentiate between UHECR compositions.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction states - smooth, rough, and intermediate - in response to surface roughness. The key difference between the intermediate and the other two states lies in the texture of the leading apex, which remains stationary during motion. Notably, the intermediate state can be achieved by coating a rough surface with a monolayer that creates a rough texture on the foam apex. This has significant implications for understanding and controlling the flow of complex liquids in various settings.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN) for the image classification task. For the metadata analysis, both univariate and multivariate methods were explored, with the decision tree algorithm proving effective. Furthermore, an interactive tool was created to assist clinicians in understanding the model's decision-making process, and it gained recognition as a runner-up in the challenge's best visualization category.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restoring forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical analysis is used to investigate positioning, curvature, thickness, angular velocity's rate of rotation, centrifugal force, tension, and radius effects on the membrane's shape, which is also modeled computationally to validate the results. At high angular velocity rates, the membrane may touch the cell's bottom, affecting the model's applicability, and an elastic membrane may develop a wedge-shaped indentation.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications.

The detection of C6H- in this molecule is the first of its kind, albeit with low signal strength, and it opens up new possibilities for observing C6H in more complex environments. The detection requires a minimum population of approximately 3×10^29 cm^-2 in the C6H molecule, which can be seen in certain conditions. The current findings suggest that the area in question may contain several hidden instances of the C6H molecule, and the sensitivity of the observation may allow the feature to be detected more clearly in the future. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Partridge suggest that a translational approach, applying computer science knowledge to enhance human well-being, could be a productive framework. From this perspective, the complexity of modern healthcare and life sciences suggests that computer science could make a substantial contribution to its solution. A focus on healthcare and biology as a means to apply and advance computer science knowledge could result in better outcomes for patients and the progression of the field.

This model has been analyzed within the framework of the phase space and the impact of different types of dissipation on the evolution of the universe has been investigated through the lens of the Hubble parameter and the deceleration parameter. Furthermore, state equation curves have been plotted to provide a comprehensive understanding of the universe's expansion. It has been shown that the universe's expansion is directly influenced by the relationship between the two components of the fluid, which has been referred to as $\Omega_{\rm dmc}$, and the behavior of the universe has been shown to be consistent with observational data for a range of values. In educational settings, curiosity plays a vital role in fostering creativity and a passion for learning.  However, traditional classroom practices often fail to nurture these qualities.  To address this shortcoming, we introduce a project called CurioBot, a chatbot that encourages curiosity through reward-based mechanisms and meta-reinforcement learning.  By utilizing reward signals that recognize and reciprocate curiosity, curious students are positively reinforced, ultimately leading to increased curiosity and engagement in challenging tasks.  We evaluated the effectiveness of CurioBot in a simulated classroom setting and found that its reward-return strategy and an integrated component called Meta-Mirror contribute to higher levels of curiosity andcreativity in its user base.  The project's results demonstrate the potential of reinforcement learning to facilitate meaningful human interaction in a classroom context.

Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are available for use in Euclidean space, there is a lack of similar models suitable for use on undirected graphs.  This research introduces two new Gaussian process models specifically for graph data, offering both efficient computation and a reliable method for uncertainty quantification.  Building upon the foundation of the sparse precision and structured covariance processes, these new models build upon the characteristics of the precision and covariance operators that characterize the Gaussian process, resulting in an efficient process that can be used for both regression and graph data.  While the first model uses the standard Laplace density and corresponds to the GPUM model, it does not provide a heavy-tailed distribution, which is why a second model with a Laplace density is also introduced.  These new processes have the potential to be used in a range of applications, including the simulation of physical systems, such as electrical circuits and mechanical systems, which often involve undirected graphs.

The effective management of urban roads is crucial for the well-being of city inhabitants. Current monitoring methods, which involve deploying automated sensors to detect and identify road incidents, are already well-established. However, the significant operational expenses associated with these systems lead to their confinement to specific urban areas. In contrast, the widespread adoption of smartphones has transformed the practice of crowd-sensing, allowing them to contribute to road monitoring and discovery. Despite the potential for crowd-sensing to monitor roads, the inherent inaccuracy of user-submitted data poses a challenge. As a result, developing efficient techniques for urban road incident detection and identification from crowd-sensed data has become a challenge. In this research, a method is proposed to analyze the dataset provided by the urban road monitoring project of Peking University, which involves the removal of duplicate entries, a task that constitutes a substantial portion of the total processing time. Furthermore, the proposed method to identify the type of road incident takes advantage of the characteristics of the dataset and the characteristics of road incidents. In addition, a linear time algorithm is designed for the purpose of filtering the dataset, achieving a remarkable improvement in processing time, which is 4 orders of magnitude faster than the raw data, and the technique for identifying the type of road incident achieves a high accuracy rate of 97.7%.

Our research explores the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To address uncertainties in dark matter production, we combined limits on J/ψ decays into invisible matter and production of light dark matter in nuclear targets from the LHC, surface and sub-surface dark matter experiments. We found that future $e^+e^-$ colliders can significantly enhance the J/ψ production cross-section, allowing for more precise measurements of J/ψ decay rates and larger data sets. This, in turn, will provide more accurate constraints on light sterile neutrinos and dark matter self-interactions. Moreover, we showed that the current invisible J/ψ decay width limit, along with production of light dark matter in nuclear targets from the NSI and CHARM experiments, results in nearly 5 sigma exclusion of a specific sterile neutrino scenario with minimal Majorana neutrino mixing.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, the MFSSA R-package is made available to facilitate the methodology discussed.

The success of automated essay scoring systems relies heavily on the extraction of relevant information from written texts and the development of effective decision models. In this study, a deep learning-based method is proposed to evaluate essays on a particular topic, using written submissions from nearly 9000 participants of a writing competition. By leveraging labeled data from the competition, the proposed method was tested and demonstrated superior performance compared to alternative approaches, as measured by a highest possible scoring metric of 1.0.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,v)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ denotes the probability that a specific type of random walk $S(t) = v_t x + \xi(t)$ is at a specific negative value at time $t$, and this random walk uses a resistance time change on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ where the steps take values in $\{-1,1\}$ with equal probability, given the step times $v_t$ have a symmetric stable distribution with parameter $\alpha$ ($\alpha \in (0,d]$). The power law decays converge if $\phi(x,v)$ converges, and for the given walk, $2-\alpha \le \phi(x,v) \le x + \alpha$. Additionally, we have further results for $\phi(x,v)$'s limiting values as $x$ approaches zero or infinity.

The ICRF test facility IASS is located at the JET site and has been recently upgraded to 250kW. A new antenna design has been implemented and has successfully operated since its installation in mid-2015. Data collected from the antenna's initial to mid 2017 will be presented. Results obtained with the new antenna show that the helicon mode was achieved and maintained throughout 14 full plasma disances, with the upgrade allowing for increased maximum power levels and better control over the antenna's internal resonators to broaden its frequency bandwidth. By reaching the helicon mode, significant improvements in plasma density and density profile were observed, resulting in enhanced plasma density and optimization of ion heating for improved ion absorption of radio waves.

In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies.

While automatic cancer diagnosis holds great promise, a significant challenge persists due to the difficulty in identifying and segmenting tumor nuclei in images. Existing methods for this task often rely on time-consuming manual annotation. To streamline this process, deep learning-based nucleus segmentation has been widely adopted, yet a critical issue remains: the lack of a standardized, high-quality dataset for training and testing these models. In this study, we introduce an innovative, high-performance nucleus segmentation dataset called PanNuke, which comprises a diverse range of cancer-diagnostic images. Consisting of 1,550 manually annotated images, each depicting varying amounts of nuclei from single to clusters of tumor cells, PanNuke has been created to support the development and assessment of advanced nucleus segmentation models. To evaluate its performance, we conducted rigorous experiments using multiple deep learning models, including Mask R-CNN combined with ResNet50 and ResNet101, as well as SOLOv1. The resulting segmentations demonstrated exceptional accuracy. Furthermore, to facilitate fair comparisons, we open-source an optimized segmentation evaluation protocol along with corresponding evaluation results.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not equal to two, along with a non-Archimedean split simply connected $p$-adic group of type $A_l$. Let $\text{B}$ be the Borel subgroup of this group. Given two distinct integral dominant weights $\lambda$ and $\mu$ for this group, we define the irreducible admissible generic representations $\sigma_\lambda$ and $\sigma_\mu$ on this group, which correspond to $\lambda$ and $\mu$ respectively in the Langlands parameterization. The question is under what conditions two such representations $\sigma_\lambda$ and $\sigma_\mu$ are isomorphic. According to the Local Langlands Correspondence, this occurs if and only if $\lambda = \mu$. However, our research provides a more specific criterion: the isomorphism between $\sigma_\lambda$ and $\sigma_\mu$ is determined by whether the set of $\text{B}$- orbits of integral dominant weights, which parameterize irreducible admissible generic $\text{B}$- orbits, for $\mu$ can be obtained from the set of $\text{B}$- orbits for $\lambda$ by multiplication by $-1$. This criterion holds for a specific class of groups, which includes $SL_{n+1}$. Xiong and Liu previously provided a definition for graphs G that have hamiltonian n-th iterated line graphs, L^n(G), where n is 2 or greater. In this study, we examine whether an L^n(G) graph possesses a hamiltonian path, and offer a definition for G to achieve this condition. Additionally, we apply this definition to set multiple upper limits for a graph's hamiltonian path index.

Cell death induced by pyroptosis is characterized as an inflammatory, immunogenic process that is resistant to apoptosis.  Among the various mechanisms leading to pyroptosis, NLRP3 inflammasome activation is the most comprehensively understood pathway.  Pyroptotic cell death is often triggered by intracellular infections or extracellular toxins that activate caspase-1 through the NLRP3 inflammasome, a process that is usually a secondary response to pyroptosis.  Once activated, the NLRP3 inflammasome induces the release of proinflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-1$\beta$ and interleukin-18, through caspase-1-mediated processes.  Ultimately, this activation results in the influx of calcium ions into cells in the form of $Ca^{2+}$ influx.  In this review, we focus on the underlying molecular pathways of pyroptosis, as well as the role of the NLRP3 inflammasome in pyroptosis, as they are relevant to cancer development.  Furthermore, we discuss the development of narcoptosis, a resistance to pyroptosis that arises from the interaction of the NLRP3 inflammasome with the narcoptotic cell death pathway through the B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2) protein. External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of this process. This acceleration could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. Two methods are devised for identifying the uncontrollable state variables, and the results from applying these methods to multiple test environments show a significant increase in the speed of these methods, as well as a faster rate when compared to the original situation.

A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, proposing a novel interpretation that views GCNNs as a form of Approximate Bayesian Inference. This interpretation allows us to derive a simplified interpretation of GCNN activations, providing a basis for a new application: using these activations to guide the optimization of ODEs. As a result, we develop a novel technique, GCNN-GODIE, which employs Approximate Bayesian Inference to produce initial values for the ODE that are informed by the network's activation distribution.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory can be reformulated as the square of the anti-de Sitter (AdS) 2-form connection for $Sp(2,2)$ gauge theory. When we add Witten's scalar solitons to this, the resulting form is compatible with the anti-self-duality of the connection, provided that the holonomy of the connection is trivial along null curves. This results in a massive modification to the standard simple spectrum of the connection. As we apply a semi-classical approximation to this system, we can derive a Schrödinger equation that includes a mass term. This allows us to obtain the anti-de Sitter bulk spectrum, which is in line with the CFT scalar mass spectrum given by the anti-de Sitter scalar mass formula. This process essentially mirrors the bulk calculation of witten's critical scalar solitons in a three-dimensional, Einstein's gravity with a negative cosmological constant.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

The traditional Synthetic Aperture (SA) method, extensively employed in ultrasound elastography, suffers from propagating noise due to the quadratic enhancement of RF data during the displacement map calculation. In an attempt to address this issue, we have developed an innovative approach based on Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) imaging. Unlike conventional SA which linearly combines the axial and lateral displacement components, the VSSA method models the wave propagation backward from the receiver to the source location. Consequently, the VSSA method compensates for signal attenuation inherent in RF data, ensue in producing displacement maps with notably lower speckle noise. Although addressing computational complexity and lateral propagation artifacts is crucial, we have demonstrated through both simulations and in-vivo experiments the superior performance of the VSSA approach in producing displacement maps with significantly lower levels of speckle noise when compared to the SA, thereby showcasing its potential for enhancing the quality of elastographic images.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves a similar purpose to Goedel's famous formulae-words equivalence, which established an important bridge between abstract mathematics and concrete reality, ultimately influencing the development of computability logic. In this context, we present a specific type of logical system, called computability logic type theory, which natural deduction serves as a prototype for. This new system establishes an alternative framework that provides both a refined understanding of the connection between algorithms and proofs and a solid foundation for a theory that unifies data types and imperative operations.

The concept of Boolean Ramsey numbers for sets of posets was initially explored in relation to Boolean lattices and posets with a single comparability pair, and a general formula was previously derived for such cases. Building upon this previous work, we have obtained a new, more universal formula related to the logarithm of 2 for Boolean Ramsey numbers. Additionally, for posets consisting of multiple disjoint pairs, we have found a more general formula that implies the earlier result. Finally, we have explored some specific cases that do not adhere to these posetal Ramsey formulas and identified cases that do not have a straightforward logarithmic growth rate.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a n-tuple in R^d is now referred to as a cyclic n-tuple, or CON for short, if the elements of the n-tuple maintain a specific, equidistant angular relationship with one another, or a maximal, or COM for short, if this condition is met with less strict requirements. A key characteristic of cyclic and near-cyclic n-tuples is that their elements form a nerongular simplex, or an equilateral-like geometric figure. Using straightforward, neurestimated bounds, near-cyclic characteristics can now be met by independent and uniformly distributed random variables, or even those following Laplacian distributions. Furthermore, Koml\'os theorem is applied to show that almost all infinite sequences, or COM almost surely, contain infinitely many near-cyclic Combinations of eight elements, or COM8 for short.

Recently, deep learning techniques, particularly the unsupervised method cycleGAN, have gained popularity in the field of CT image denoising due to their capability to handle paired and unpaired data. Typically, cycleGAN models employ two separate generators to transform low-dose (LDC) images into high-dose (HDC) ones and vice versa. In this study, we propose a novel modified cycleGAN architecture by using a single switchable generator that can perform the transformation in both directions. By conducting the same weight updates during backward propagation, we ensure that the model learns an optimal solution to convert one type of image to another. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we carried out a series of numerical experiments on a pair of LDC and HDC images. The results demonstrate that our modified cycleGAN achieves comparable, if not superior, performance to the original cycleGAN model.

Recent advancements in neural network-based understanding of conversations have achieved significant success in dialogue tasks, yet many current models treat dialogue histories as linear sequences, neglecting the inherent hierarchical structure of conversations. To address this limitation, we introduce a tree-based neural network model, which leverages a pre-trained conversation structure to enhance dialogue comprehension. This study explores various methods to integrate the conversation tree into neural network models and presents a straightforward approach to neural pruning that yields state-of-the-art results on multiple dialog understanding evaluation metrics. Additionally, our model's robustness and efficiency are demonstrated through additional experiments and the potential for horizontal scaling is  explored through a car learning method that outperforms the current state-of-the-art and demonstrates the effectiveness of using hierarchical representations in conversations.

This research aims to examine the geometric makeup of an ideal fluid's spacetime 
when coupled with a torsion-forming vector field and the relationship between the 
conformal Ricci-Yamabe metric and the conformal eta-Ricci-Yamabe metric. We first 
derive conditions for the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton to be in a state of 
expansion, stability, or contraction. Subsequently, we establish a Laplace 
equation using the conformal eta-Ricci-Yamabe soliton when the soliton's potential 
vector field is a gradient type. Additionally, this research relates an ideal 
fluid's spacetime to a Robertson-Walker spacetime and discusses various physics 
and gravitational implications.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that deformed halo structures endure from intrinsic ground states to collective rotational states, particularly illustrating shape decoupling effects in rotating distorted halo nuclei.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, as it effectively utilizes temporal information, but its application is hindered by memory limitations and real-time processing requirements, necessitating the removal of these components. To maintain their applications without these limitations, we develop a novel multi-path network, incorporating two innovative modules: one that propagates feature information through second-order grid transformation, and another that achieves deformable temporal alignment guided by flow orientation. Our design automatically extracts flow information from the input, realigns subsequent frames based on this information, and utilizes the grid propagation module to connect spatially aligned features across frames, effectively capturing the flow-guided grid features that serve as an implicit prior for motion information. As a result, our model surpasses the current state-of-the-art results in video super-resolution, achieving exceptional performance on benchmark tests, and is particularly advantageous for applications involving motion information extraction, optical flow learning, and flow-aware video enhancement. The source code for the network is available on GitHub.

Due to the possibility of nonperturbative effects in lepton colliders operating above a few TeV, there needs to be a thorough investigation of the associated black disks that arise from them. A detailed examination of the implications these have for the future lepton colliders, particularly for ILC, CLIC, FCC-ee, and DLHC, has been conducted in this study. The probability distribution of the disk radius and transverse momentum that arise from both the photon and the gluon have been derived from the gluon content of the polarized gluon distribution function and the non-Abelian nature of QCD respectively. A depth profile function that accounts for the decreasing density of downstream particles has been developed to provide a more accurate assessment of the disk effect. The implications of this investigation for the design of future lepton colliders has led to the consideration of disk collimators in the machine design, a shift from the previously assumed point-like interaction in the physics design, the installation of shielding to protect nearby experiments from the disk, and a thorough examination of the disk effect on the physics potential of biased physics studies conducted in this investigation.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods, incorporating it into model-based
reinforcement learning presents additional challenges, particularly when
training shared world models due to data divergence. This research proposes a
novel approach that unifies multiple task-specific models under a single world
model through a selective knowledge aggregation mechanism. By doing so, the
method effectively pools knowledge from both the relevant and irrelevant tasks
in the WATMAN framework. It shows that by removing the data from the irrelevant
tasks during the choice of training data, the model can achieve a more robust
and efficient learning process. Experimental results demonstrate that WATMAN
outperforms other models in terms of both accuracy and efficiency in the
complex environment of Minecraft.

The paper provides derivations of Li-Yau and Souplet-Zhang type estimates for the equation $u_t=\Delta_\xi p + \lambda u + A(u)$ in a complete, non-compact metric measure space with compact boundary. Furthermore, the paper includes local gradient estimates for the equation $\Delta_\xi(u^p)+\lambda u + A(u) = 0$ on complete, non-compact manifolds with compact boundary.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

When the population is not fully known in advance, sampling occurs in sequence, either individually or in batches, which are obtained sequentially. This work presents a novel algorithm that allows for sequential selection of a balanced sample. The algorithm accommodates equal and unequal inclusion probabilities and can also be applied to select spatially balanced samples when the population contains geographical coordinates. Moreover, an investigation using simulated data reveals that the proposed method surpasses alternative methods.

In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task. We have assessed the effectiveness of various approaches to calibrating cameras using only images, including traditional methods, deep-learning-based techniques, and a comprehensive survey of semi-supervised and self-supervised strategies that combine images with other sensor data. These approaches often involve training models using pre-existing datasets to integrate visual and sensor information, or developing innovative techniques to incorporate such data in real-time applications. We have organized the described approaches based on the construction of camera positions and orientations, and highlighted the benefits and limitations of each method, and identified potential future research directions.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This process often involves sampling from the posterior distribution, but existing methods are limited in their ability to efficiently generate high-quality results. We introduce an innovative approach that leverages a latent diffusion model, which is trained to represent the posterior and enables rapid generation of images through the noise-to-signal process. Rather than directly modeling the image, we apply a clever strategy that uses a degraded observation to gradually transform a random noise image into a clean one, effectively balancing data fidelity and prior feasibility. This approach yields superior results on real-world degraded images, particularly in recovering complex structures, and efficiently runs on CPU, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches in both speed and accuracy. Our method's effectiveness across various real-world images and its computational advantages make it a promising solution in inverse problems.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that can only be achieved through terahertz communication. To facilitate this, outdoor directional beamforming is being developed for Terahertz Pan-Tiltable Antenna (TPA) systems featuring dual-reconfigurable beamforming capabilities. A key objective of this study is developing an efficient algorithm to determine optimal TPAs by considering power constraints in order to maximize desired signal strength while minimizing interference. To address this challenge, a low-complexity algorithm is designed by transforming the problem into a more manageable form, which only necessitates simple calculations. Simulation results demonstrate the algorithm's simplicity and accuracy when compared to optimal solutions and existing methods. Furthermore, the article explores the impact of reconfigurable antennas on performance, shedding light on the $30$ GHz center frequency phenomenon.
